entry.title: FasterTransformer Source Tour: The CUDA Kernel Lab Behind Modern LLM Serving

link.title: FasterTransformer Source Tour: The CUDA Kernel Lab Behind Modern LLM Serving

entry.content:
Between 2019 and 2022, if you wanted transformer inference to actually go fast on NVIDIA GPUs, you ended up reading FasterTransformer. It was NVIDIA’s C++/CUDA laboratory for the transformer block: attention, FFN, layernorm, sampling, and weight quantization treated as kernel-engineering problems rather than framework conveniences. It shipped encoder paths for BERT, decoder and decoding paths for machine translation, and a full GPT serving stack with bindings for TensorFlow, PyTorch, and a Triton backend. One honest note before anything else: the repository is frozen. The very first line of its README states that development has transitioned to TensorRT-LLM and that the repo “will not have further development.” Everything below should be read as a blueprint from that archive, not as a living project.

Why spend a post on frozen code? Because the blueprints escaped. The decode-time multi-head attention kernel we will visit is a direct ancestor of the one vLLM launched with, and its custom allreduce idea reappeared in TensorRT-LLM and vLLM almost unchanged in spirit. Its weight-only-quantization GEMM scaffolding, built on CUTLASS (a codebase we toured separately here), foreshadowed the entire W4A16 wave that ktransformers-style hybrid inference rides today. Reading FasterTransformer is reading the lab notebook that modern serving systems copied from.

This post walks the GPT serving path from a Triton model config down to a single CUDA kernel launch, using two diagrams generated directly from the src/fastertransformer tree on branch main: a compact overview first, and a detailed 34-node map later in the post. Every line anchor we link was verified against the working tree. If you want a warm-up on why token-level serving matters at all, our inference overview and the Triton Inference Server tour are good companions.

Overview of the FasterTransformer GPT serving stack: a Triton model builder instantiates the ParallelGpt engine, which drives context and step decoders over tensor-parallel attention and FFN layers, backed by fused kernels, custom allreduce, and a cuBLAS wrapper.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • ParallelGptTritonModel, L306 — the serving entry point; it parses a Triton config.ini, weights, and MPI world size, then spawns one engine per GPU and hands out model instances.
  • ParallelGpt::forward, L534 — the top-level engine loop: prefill over the prompt, then one step per generated token, sampling, stopping, and tensor-parallel logit gathers.
  • ParallelGptContextDecoder::forward, L303 — the prefill pass, which pushes all prompt tokens through the block stack at once and fills the KV cache.
  • ParallelGptDecoder::forward, L257 — the incremental step decoder, invoked once per token at L1346 of ParallelGpt.cc.
  • TensorParallelGptContextAttentionLayer::forward, L23 and TensorParallelDecoderSelfAttentionLayer::forward, L185 — thin wrappers that shard attention GEMMs across ranks and allreduce the partial outputs.
  • TensorParallelGeluFfnLayer::forward, L33 — the column-parallel/row-parallel FFN sandwich around FfnLayer::forward, L34.
  • masked_multihead_attention, L72 — the famous single-kernel decode attention, called from DecoderSelfAttentionLayer.cc, L144.
  • oneShotAllReduceKernel, L139 — the custom allreduce over P2P-mapped peer buffers, with NCCL (ftNcclAllReduceSum, L56) as the fallback.
  • invokeTopKSampling, L439 — curand-seeded top-k/top-p token selection at the end of each step.

The detailed map: 34 nodes from Triton instances and the PyTorch op through the GPT engine, tensor-parallel layers, and the kernel layer — the same structure the rest of this post follows.

A Tensor Class That Carries Its Own Memory Type

The root abstraction is small. struct Tensor at L107 is a pointer plus a data type, a shape, and a memory-type tag (CPU, GPU, or framework-owned), with helpers to convert to and from PyTorch and TensorFlow tensors. A TensorMap is then just a string-keyed bag of tensors, and it becomes the calling convention for every layer: layers read inputs and write outputs by name. That is the entire interface glue, and it is why the same C++ core can be driven by three different frameworks.

Below the tensors sits an allocator hierarchy. IAllocator at L64 has specializations for raw CUDA allocation, PyTorch’s allocator, and TensorFlow’s BTF allocator, all exposing the same malloc/free/reMalloc surface with a shared pooling idea: freed device buffers are cached by size class rather than returned to CUDA immediately. Every layer inherits a buffer-lifecycle contract from BaseLayer’s allocateBuffer at L54, and small utilities like deviceMalloc at L29 fill the gaps. This design is invisible from Python but explains a lot of the speed: there is no hidden host-device synchronization at layer boundaries, because the memory contract is explicit.

The PyTorch side of the bridge is GptOp::forward at L106, a custom op that converts torch::Tensor inputs into ft::Tensor, calls the engine, and converts outputs back. If you have read our PyTorch extension material, this is the heavyweight industrial version of the same pattern.

The Decode Kernel Everyone Copied

GPT generation is memory-bound: for each new token, the model reads every weight once and performs little arithmetic. FasterTransformer’s most influential attack on that problem was to collapse an entire incremental attention step — reading the QKV projection, adding bias, applying rotary-free positional state, computing softmax against the cached keys, and appending the new K/V to the cache — into a single CUDA kernel per layer. The launcher is masked_multihead_attention at L72, and the actual GPU code is a template, masked_multihead_attention_kernel at L1119, instantiated per head dimension in sibling files sized from 32 up to 256.

The kernel keeps a query vector in registers, streams over cached keys and values in shared-memory tiles, and writes the updated cache slot — no intermediate global-memory round trip for attention scores. This is the kernel that vLLM’s early versions shipped a port of, and its one-warp-per-head layout is recognizable in several successor projects. It is also the reason the file tree looks the way it does: a directory of per-head-size instantiations generated from one template, so nvcc can compile each shape at its best register pressure.

The prefill (context) path is a different beast because sequence lengths are large and compute-bound, so it runs a more conventional multi-stage flow: GptContextAttentionLayer::forward at L25 runs one fused QKV GEMM through the cuBLAS wrapper, then invokeAddFusedQKVBiasTranspose at L1502 applies bias and splits heads in a single pass, and a masked softmax follows. For encoder models the repo goes further and calls into TensorRT’s fused flash-attention cubins under 3rdparty/trt_fused_multihead_attention — the same family of techniques our FlashAttention tour covers from the research side.

Tensor Parallelism Without the Tax

The multi-GPU GPT lives under models/multi_gpu_gpt, and its structure is a case study in how little code tensor parallelism actually needs if the layers cooperate. The block-stack constructors wire themselves up in a few lines — ParallelGptDecoder.cc at L27 creates a TensorParallelDecoderSelfAttentionLayer and at L44 a TensorParallelGeluFfnLayer — and from there every GEMM is head-sharded or column-sharded, followed by an allreduce of partial sums.

The interesting part is the allreduce backend. The default is NCCL, initialized in ftNcclInitialize at L308 and invoked through ftNcclAllReduceSum at L56; the engine also allgathers final logits across the tensor-parallel group so every rank can sample the same next token. But NCCL’s per-call overhead hurts at decode-time batch sizes, so FasterTransformer added its own allreduce: peer GPUs map each other’s device memory with P2P APIs, CustomAllReduceComm::customAllReduce at L46 negotiates the peer pointers and swaps in an internal buffer, and then either oneShotAllReduceKernel at L139 or twoShotAllReduceKernel at L202 finishes the reduction in a single kernel launch. DeepSpeed later popularized a near-identical mechanism, which we looked at in the DeepSpeed tour.

Sampling and stopping are their own kernel zoo: invokeTopPSampling at L1208 for nucleus sampling, beam_online_softmax_topk_kernel at L297 for streaming beam search, invokeGatherTree at L636 to backtrace finished beams into sequences, and invokeLengthCriterion at L135 to mark EOS and max-length stops on-device.

From Install to Your First Model

The documented path in docs/gpt_guide.md is container-first, and that is still the most reliable way to build it. Start from a recent NGC PyTorch container (the guide uses nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:22.09-py3-era images), clone the repository, and pull its submodules — git submodule init && git submodule update — since the CUTLASS-based kernels and the TensorRT fused-attention assets live in 3rdparty. Then build with CMake, selecting your GPU’s compute capability:

mkdir build && cd build
cmake -DSM=80 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_PYT=ON -DBUILD_MULTI_GPU=ON ..
make -j12

-DBUILD_PYT=ON produces the PyTorch custom op; -DBUILD_MULTI_GPU=ON enables the tensor-parallel path; dropping -DBUILD_PYT and adding the TensorFlow flag builds that binding instead. Before running anything, do what every FasterTransformer user ritualistically did: run the GEMM sweep, generate_gpt_gemm_config at L27, which benchmarks cuBLAS candidates across your shapes and writes the winners into gemm_config.ini — for example ./bin/gpt_gemm 8 1 32 12 128 6144 51200 1 1 0 for a GPT-2-XL-shaped sweep. At runtime cublasMMWrapper::Gemm at L94 consults that cache per shape, which is why a model without a tuned config can be noticeably slower.

For a first end-to-end run, convert a Megatron- or HuggingFace-format GPT-2 checkpoint into FT’s split format, point examples/cpp/multi_gpu_gpt/gpt_config.ini at it (that file controls model path, tensor-parallel size, and decoding hyper-parameters), and run ./bin/multi_gpu_gpt_example on one GPU or mpirun -n 8 ./bin/multi_gpu_gpt_example across eight. The PyTorch route is the same idea through the op: python ../examples/pytorch/gpt/multi_gpu_gpt_example.py --tensor_para_size=8 --ckpt_path=.... For actual serving, the Triton backend builds into a shared library you drop into a Triton model repository; the model config maps one-to-one onto what ParallelGptTritonModel reads. Our Triton Inference Server overview explains the server side of that contract, and TGI represents where that serving layer went next.

Weights, LayerNorm, and the Plumbing Nobody Photographs

Two supporting cast members deserve a mention. Weight loading is split cleanly: ParallelGptWeight::loadModel at L293 reads embeddings and the output kernel, while ParallelGptDecoderLayerWeight::loadModel at L275 reads each layer’s QKV, FFN, and layernorm tensors, with INT8 and FP8 variants handled by sibling weight classes. Around the two big GEMMs of every block, small fused kernels do the glue work on-device: invokeGeneralLayerNorm at L1653 (RMSNorm included, which is how the repo supported NeoX-style variants), invokeGenericActivation at L243 fusing bias and GELU/Silu into the FFN middle product, and invokeAddBiasResidual at L55 for the residual adds. Embedding lookup with positional encoding and prompt-past splicing lives in gpt_kernels.cu at L120. None of these is glamorous; together they are the reason a GPT step touches DRAM once per tensor instead of three times. For contrast, nanoGPT and llm.c are excellent minimal implementations that make FT’s engineering density obvious.

Honest Limits

Read the archive banner first: the README’s opening line says FasterTransformer transitioned to TensorRT-LLM and will receive no further development. The last commits date to 2023-era dependencies, and the FP8 work targets Hopper-era CUDA 11.8 images. Nothing here tracks newer architectures, MLA-style attention, or speculative decoding.

Build complexity is real. Submodule pulls, per-architecture SM flags, and template instantiation per dtype and head dimension make for long compiles and large binaries. The C++ API is heavy for the same reasons the kernels are fast: you assemble TensorMaps by hand, size activation buffers through the allocator, configure gemm_config.ini per shape, and wire MPI yourself. There is no runtime kernel autotuning of the kind modern SGLang-style stacks take for granted. Quantization is powerful but hardware-gated — INT8 paths need Turing or newer, FP8 needs Hopper — and the support matrix in the README is explicit about which framework binding gets which feature.

Finally, the world moved on. TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA’s sanctioned successor, and the kernel ideas survive there and in vLLM; CTranslate2, TGI, and SGLang cover the practical serving space with far less ceremony. But as a map of how far careful kernel engineering pushed transformer inference before the modern frameworks existed, FasterTransformer remains one of the most instructive trees you can clone — a frozen lab, and a blueprint everyone’s serving stack still carries traces of.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of NVIDIA FasterTransformer's GPT serving stack: tensor-parallel layers, the masked multi-head attention kernel, custom allreduce, and the documented build path.

entry.title: JAX Source Tour: Tracing to Execution

link.title: JAX Source Tour: Tracing to Execution

entry.content:
Most numerical Python gives you two bad choices. Either you write eager code that is easy to debug but slow, or you write a static graph that is fast but alien. JAX’s answer is a third road: keep writing NumPy-style Python, but capture it — trace it — into a small, serializable intermediate representation the moment you ask for speed. That capture step is why the same grad, jit and vmap decorators work unchanged from a laptop CPU to a TPU pod. Where PyTorch’s runtime, which we covered in the PyTorch source tour, records ops while they execute, JAX re-executes your Python function with tracer objects and records a pure program instead.

In this post we walk the google/jax source tree (version 0.12.1 at the time of writing) along one axis only: what happens between @jax.jit on your function and device buffers coming back. That path runs through four neighborhoods — the public API, the tracing machinery that builds a jaxpr, the MLIR/XLA lowering and compilation stage, and the sharded execution runtime. The C++ half of the project, jaxlib, lives mostly outside the Python tree we will link here, but you will see its fingerprints in jax._src.lib, the extension module that wraps the XLA client.

If you have read our pieces on ONNX graph interchange or on tinygrad, the jaxpr will feel familiar: it is a flat, SSA-style list of equations, much closer to an ONNX graph than to Python. The difference is that JAX never asks you to write that graph. The Python source is the front end, and everything below it is infrastructure you can read like any other program.

Overview of the JAX source, from the public API through tracing, lowering and compilation down to sharded execution. Generated from the repository tree of google/jax on branch main.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at jit, L187 in the public API module — and despite the name, it immediately hands off to make_jit, L453 in the pjit module. Modern JAX has exactly one implementation of “compile this function”, and jit is a thin shell over it.
  • Argument handling happens twice: once as Python-level flattening in flatten_fun, L72, and once as pytree decomposition in tree_flatten, L86. JAX sees your dict of parameters as a tree of leaves plus a treedef, and that structure survives all the way into the compiled artifact.
  • The transformation stack lives in WrappedFun, L145: every transform (grad, vmap, remat) wraps the function with parameters that the tracer consults later, so transforms compose by nesting wrappers rather than by editing code.
  • Tracing itself is JaxprTrace, L116: a Python interpreter that follows your function while collecting JaxprEqn, L411 nodes into a Jaxpr, L99.
  • Autodiff is not a second system — linearize, L227 re-traces your function under a JVP tracer and reuses the same partial-evaluation machinery, which is why grad and jit compose in any order.
  • Lowering turns the jaxpr into an MLIR module inside StableHLO dialects at lower_jaxpr_to_module, L1394, using per-primitive rules registered by the lax library.
  • Compilation is compile_or_get_cached, L436: it resolves the platform client through get_backend, L980, checks the persistent cache, and otherwise ships the module to XLA.
  • Execution has two doors: the eager op-by-op path in apply_primitive, L82 (which, amusingly, works by jitting each single primitive), and the sharded path, where shard_args, L86 slices inputs across the mesh before a MeshExecutable runs.
  • What comes back is an ArrayImpl, L226: a NumPy-like object that is really a bag of device buffers, each with its own sharding.

Tracing: Where Python Becomes a Graph

The core trick deserves a closer look, because everything else in JAX is built on it. A tracer is a stand-in value that records every operation applied to it. When you call a jitted function, JAX wraps your arguments in tracers, runs your Python code, and harvests the record. The result is the jaxpr: invariants in, constants folded in, and a straight-line list of equations, each naming a primitive, its inputs and its outputs. You can see one yourself without any ceremony:

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def f(x):
    return jnp.sin(x) * 2.0

print(jax.make_jaxpr(f)(jnp.zeros((3,))))

That output — make_jaxpr is defined at make_jaxpr, L2194 — is a real data structure you can pass around, transform and inspect. Control flow like lax.scan and lax.while_loop shows up as higher-order equations holding nested jaxprs, which is precisely why Python for loops over data do not survive tracing: the tracer only sees unrolled operations unless you reach for those primitives. Each equation’s meaning is defined twice, once abstractly and once concretely; the concrete evaluator is eval_jaxpr, L748, which is what runs when you ask for eager execution.

Primitives are declared in one place and given rules everywhere else, and the lax library is the registry. Look at how a basic op is assembled at add_p, L5524: a primitive object, then three lines that attach its JVP rule to ad.primitive_jvps, its transposition rule to ad.primitive_transposes, and its XLA lowering via mlir.register_lowering. Every transform you use is a dictionary lookup against tables like these. This separation — one primitive, many small rules — is the quiet design decision that makes the whole system composable, and it is a pattern worth stealing for your own DSLs. Source provenance is not lost either: equations carry file/line data through SourceInfo, L136, so stack traces through three nested transforms still point at your original line of Python.

Autodiff and the Transform Stack

Because grad is “run the tracer, then differentiate the jaxpr”, JAX autodiff is source-to-source in spirit even though it never touches your Python text. linearize, L227 splits a function into its primal pass and a linear part; transposition turns the linear part around to get vector-Jacobian products. Reverse-mode differentiation of a jaxpr is effectively a clever backwards interpreter over the same equation list, which is why memory, not speed, is the binding constraint — the whole primal trace stays live until the backward pass consumes it.

That constraint has an elegant fix: jax.checkpoint (remat) is defined at remat, L393 and works by re-tracing the forward function inside the backward pass, trading recomputation for memory. It composes with everything because it is implemented through the same partial-evaluation hooks as any other transform. The same story repeats for vmap: BatchTrace, L232 adds a batch dimension to every operation via per-primitive batching rules, and custom rules hook in through the same primitive tables. Even user-defined derivatives, declared with custom_jvp, L87, integrate by registering rules rather than by special-casing.

If you have trained models with transformers or ported a nanogpt loop, this is the machinery you were using: loss = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn) is two nested tracers deep before it ever touches XLA. And when you stack jit(grad(vmap(f))), you are literally nesting WrappedFun wrappers — the design keeps each layer dumb and the composition correct.

From Jaxpr to Silicon: Lowering and Compilation

The jaxpr leaves Python-land at the MLIR boundary. lower_jaxpr_to_module walks the equations and calls each primitive’s registered lowering rule, which typically emits StableHLO operations; constants become embedded literals via ir_constants, L285 machinery around it. You can drop from this level to hand-written kernels when needed — mixing in Triton via jax.experimental.pallas or shaping how XLA fuses things — but the default path assumes XLA will do the fusion, layout and scheduling work that a hand-tuned stack like CUTLASS does manually.

Compilation proper is where the C++ world takes over. compile_or_get_cached, L436 gathers compile options at get_compile_options, L187, consults the persistent cache — keys built in VerificationCache, L131 — and finally calls backend_compile_and_load against a client obtained from the backend registry. That registry, xla_bridge, maps a platform string ("cpu", "gpu", "tpu") to a lazily-initialized XLA client; get_backend at get_backend, L980 is the doorway. In architecture terms this is the same boundary an ONNX Runtime execution provider or an IREE target backend occupies — compare our onnxruntime and IREE tours — except JAX’s “graph format” is the jaxpr-to-StableHLO lowering rather than a serialized file.

One detail worth appreciating: compilation is keyed on shapes, dtypes, sharding and static arguments, not on values. That is why the first call to a jitted function is slow and every structurally identical call after it is free, and why changing a Python int that was marked static_argnums silently triggers a recompile.

From Install to Your First Model

The CPU wheel is a two-liner, and the CUDA one is only slightly longer:

pip install -U jax            # CPU only
pip install -U "jax[cuda12]"  # NVIDIA GPU plugin wheels

Everything shown below uses only stable public API — the same calls that appear in the library’s own docstrings:

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

key = jax.random.key(0)                      # explicit PRNG state
params = {"w": jax.random.normal(key, (3,)),
          "b": jnp.zeros(())}

def loss(params, x, y):
    pred = x @ params["w"] + params["b"]
    return jnp.mean((pred - y) ** 2)

x = jax.random.normal(key, (64, 3))
y = jnp.ones((64,))

grad_fn = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss))            # grad composed with jit
g = grad_fn(params, x, y)
step = jax.tree.map(lambda p, e: p - 0.1 * e, params, g)
print(jax.jit(loss)(params, x, y))

Three things to notice. First, jax.random.key(0) returns an explicit key array — the PRNG type defined at PRNGKeyArray, L142, backed by the counter-based threefry_2x32, L243 bit generator. Randomness is a first-class, splittable value instead of a global generator, which is what makes seeded, reproducible training across devices tractable. Second, grad handled the dictionary params transparently because gradients flow through pytrees. Third, the update used jax.tree.map rather than a loop: under jit, ordinary Python iteration over data would be unrolled into the trace. From here, adding a real model is just more jnp — and if you want to see where such a loop goes when it grows up, our inference and vLLM pieces cover the serving side of the same ecosystem.

Sharding: One Function, Many Devices

JAX’s scaling story is not a separate API bolted on the side; it is metadata on the same jaxpr. You describe a logical Mesh, L235 of devices, annotate arrays with a NamedSharding, L71 that names mesh axes, and let the compiler insert the collectives. pjit — the engine underneath jit — traces your function, propagates sharding constraints through the jaxpr, and compiles one program whose inputs and outputs may live split across the whole mesh. Inside the runtime, shard_args, L86 handles slicing host-side inputs into per-device buffers, and the executable that comes back is a MeshExecutable, L1846 that fans the launch out across devices.

For per-shard programming, shard_map, L106 drops you one level down: your function runs on each slice with explicit collective primitives for communication. This is the mental model behind large-scale training and serving on TPUs — the same “partition the tensors, minimize the chatter” problem that ZeRO-style optimizers such as DeepSpeed solve for the PyTorch world, but expressed as compiler-visible annotations instead of runtime wrappers. The payoff is that resharding between two operations is inferred by the compiler rather than hand-written, and an ArrayImpl, L226 hides whether it is replicated, split, or scattered across an entire pod.

Honest Limits

The tracing model is powerful, and it is also the source of every common complaint. Tracing only sees values’ shapes and dtypes, so data-dependent Python control flow (if x > 0: on an array, for over data) either fails or unrolls; you must express real control flow with lax.while_loop and lax.scan, which is a genuine change of habit. Every new shape is a new compilation, so workloads with dynamic sequence lengths pay recompile taxes unless you pad or bucket — JIT-friendly design is a skill, not a default. The first call latency of a large jitted function can be seconds, since the whole lowering-to-XLA path runs synchronously, and error messages arriving from deep inside compiled code are much better than they used to be but still speak StableHLO dialect rather than Python. Eager mode exists, but it is best treated as a debugging tool, not a production mode. Memory predictability cuts both ways: because reverse-mode keeps the primal trace alive, OOMs arrive unless you plan remat and donation deliberately. And while the public NumPy surface is famously stable, the internals we toured — pxla, pjit internals, the lowering cache — move constantly; link against them at your peril. None of these are disqualifying, but they explain why JAX feels different in the hand from eager frameworks: you are not calling an operator library, you are writing programs for a compiler, and the source tree we just walked makes that explicit at every layer.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the JAX source tree: how jit traces Python into jaxprs, how autodiff and vmap ride the same tracer, and how MLIR, XLA, pjit and pxla carry your function onto the device.

entry.title: MLX Source Tour: A NumPy-Shaped Array Library with a Unified Metal/CPU Backend

link.title: MLX Source Tour: A NumPy-Shaped Array Library with a Unified Metal/CPU Backend

entry.content:
MLX is Apple’s array framework for machine learning on Apple silicon, and it occupies an interesting spot in the ecosystem. Next to PyTorch it looks deliberately small; next to JAX it shares the functional taste — function transformations like grad, vmap, and compile are first-class — but it ships with a C++ core that speaks Metal natively rather than sitting on an existing accelerator stack. If you have read our tours of llama.cpp or GGML, you have seen what it takes to hand-roll GPU execution for inference. MLX attacks the same hardware from the opposite direction: a clean NumPy-shaped user surface on top of a graph evaluator, so research code and inference code end up looking alike.

The design bet is unified memory. On an M-series machine there is one pool of RAM visible to both CPU and GPU, so MLX can move work between the two without staging copies through host memory. That single hardware fact explains most of the architecture: a tiny Device abstraction, ops that build a graph lazily, and a scheduler that interleaves CPU and Metal work on per-device streams. Compared with heavyweight serving stacks like vLLM or the minimalism of tinygrad, MLX sits in a sweet spot: a real C++ engine, but small enough to read in an afternoon.

This tour walks that engine as it exists at version 0.32.5. The repository splits cleanly into mlx/ — the C++ core with its backends — and python/ — the nanobind bindings plus the pure-Python mlx.nn and mlx.optimizers packages. We will follow an operation from Python call to Metal kernel and back, then close with what the code genuinely cannot do today.

MLX overview: Python ops append primitives to a graph of arrays; the lazy evaluator walks that graph and hands each node to the CPU or Metal backend, coordinated by the stream scheduler over a shared buffer allocator.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Every tensor is an array — the class comment says it plainly: an array is really a node in a graph, carrying shape, strides, dtype, and edges to its inputs.
  • A Device is just cpu or gpu plus an index, and a Stream is an ordered lane on that device; every primitive is bound to one.
  • Calls like add() in mlx/ops.cpp do no math — they broadcast inputs, promote dtypes, and return a new node holding an Add primitive.
  • Each Primitive must implement both eval_cpu and eval_gpu; that dual contract is the whole “unified backend” story.
  • Nothing runs until eval_impl in mlx/transforms.cpp walks the graph depth-first and dispatches each node to gpu::eval or cpu::eval.
  • The Scheduler owns one worker thread per stream and throttles the tape when too many tasks or too many bytes are in flight.
  • On the GPU side, metal::Device wraps MTL::Device with caches of Metal libraries and compiled compute-kernel states, while a MetalAllocator recycles buffers under a memory limit.
  • Python sees all of this through a nanobind module built in python/src/mlx.cpp, with mlx.nn layers as thin wrappers that trace mx calls.

Core Objects: array, Device, Stream

The C++ core is refreshingly flat. mlx/array.h defines the central type in about five hundred lines: an array is a shared descriptor with a shape of int32_t, strides, a dtype, a status flag, and — crucially — a pointer to the primitive that computes it plus the vector of input arrays. Those inputs are the graph edges. Allocation is delegated to a process-wide allocator() interface, which means the core never knows whether a buffer comes from malloc or from a Metal heap.

Device and Stream complete the vocabulary. A Device is two enums wide, and a Stream is an index paired with a device. Streams matter because they are the unit of concurrency: each thread can have its own default stream, mx.new_stream(device) mints another lane, and work submitted to different streams can overlap on the GPU. Cross-stream ordering is handled by an Event type — a wait/signal pair that the evaluator attaches to arrays flowing between streams. This is the same mental model as CUDA streams, but with no vendor library behind it; the CPU backend simply treats a stream as a worker thread.

Ops, Primitives, and the Two-Backend Contract

The user-facing surface lives in mlx/ops.cpp, a four-thousand-line catalogue of NumPy-style operations from arange to einsum. Reading any one of them shows the pattern. add() at line 3266 promotes the two inputs to a common dtype, broadcasts them, and constructs the output array with a shared pointer to an Add primitive — no arithmetic anywhere. Even matmul is just validation plus node construction. Laziness is total: a thousand lines of Python-like array code can execute in microseconds because it only sketches the graph.

The interesting file is mlx/primitives.h. The base Primitive declares pure-virtual eval_cpu and eval_gpu over vectors of inputs and outputs, and documents that the evaluation function is responsible for allocating its own output storage — donation and buffer reuse fall out of that rule. Most ops derive from UnaryPrimitive, an adapter for single-output nodes that forwards the vector form to a simpler (inputs, out) signature. Beyond evaluation, primitives optionally carry vjp, jvp, and vmap rules, which is how reverse-mode autodiff and vectorized mapping stay pure library code rather than compiler magic.

A separate layer, mlx/fast.cpp, adds fused operations — rms_norm, layer_norm, rope — each with a hand-written custom backward. These are the ops transformer models from nanoGPT-style codebases call in their hot loop, and MLX implements them once, with both CPU and Metal paths, instead of hoping a generic kernel fusion pass will invent them.

The Lazy Eval Loop and Its Scheduler

Everything converges on eval_impl in mlx/transforms.cpp. Given output arrays, it first runs a depth-first pass that records each node’s fan-in degree, then flattens the traversal into a tape in breadth-first order — with a width limit so a pathological graph does not blow up the queue. Before executing, it inserts fences wherever consecutive tape nodes switch streams, and events for ordering across separate asynchronous evaluations.

The execution loop is the heart of the system, at line 272: for each node on the tape, if the primitive’s device is GPU it calls gpu::eval, otherwise cpu::eval. That single if is where “unified Metal/CPU backend” is decided, one node at a time. The GPU branch does not block; it encodes a command buffer and returns immediately, so the tape keeps unrolling while the GPU chews. Two conditions force a pause: too many active tasks, or active memory crossing the configured limit — then the loop calls scheduler::wait_for_one() until pressure drops. The same file also hosts the transformations users see: grad() is built on value_and_grad by tracing with tracer arrays, and compile() runs graph simplify and fuse passes and caches the result keyed by shapes and mode.

The CPU branch of the contract is almost anticlimactic. cpu::eval invokes the primitive’s eval_cpu synchronously — SIMD kernels and hand-tuned GEMMs under mlx/backend/cpu/ — then dispatches a no-op task to the stream’s encoder purely to release donated buffers on the worker thread. The asymmetry is the point: the CPU is the fast path with nothing to schedule, and the GPU is the async path that needs fencing.

Inside the Metal Backend

The Metal backend under mlx/backend/metal/ is the largest single directory in the core, and its entry point is the GPU hook gpu::eval implemented in mlx/backend/metal/eval.cpp. For each array it resolves the stream’s CommandEncoder — an object that batches many kernel dispatches into one MTL::CommandBuffer, inserts barriers only when dependencies require them, and commits when a size threshold is hit. The actual call is one line: arr.primitive().eval_gpu(...) at line 45, followed by an async commit whose completion callback tells the scheduler the task finished.

Per-op GPU code lives in mlx/backend/metal/primitives.cpp and friends; for example Arange::eval_gpu figures out grid dimensions and records the matching kernel. The kernels themselves are Metal Shading Language sources — the Steel GEMM family in mlx/backend/metal/kernels/steel/ is the flagship, with tiled fused matmuls specialized per architecture generation, instantiated from templates in steel_gemm_fused.metal and dispatched by steel_matmul_regular_axpby_nax. If you enjoyed the tiling tour through CUTLASS or the fused-attention work in FlashAttention, this is Apple’s in-house answer to the same problem.

Memory management closes the loop. MetalAllocator implements the core’s Allocator interface with a buffer cache: freed GPU buffers are parked and reused by size class, with configurable cache and memory limits and peak tracking exposed through mx.metal.get_cache_memory() and friends. The evaluator consults those statistics between tape nodes — that is how a model larger than the free budget degrades gracefully instead of aborting.

From Install to Your First Model

There is no build step on Apple silicon; the PyPI wheel carries the compiled core:

pip install mlx

The two-line demo that shows the whole machine:

import mlx.core as mx

a = mx.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
b = mx.array([4.0, 5.0, 6.0])
c = a + b + 1.0      # graph node - nothing has executed yet
mx.eval(c)           # DFS tape -> CPU or Metal, per node
print(c)             # array([6, 8, 10], dtype=float32)

Between those lines, mx.eval — bound at line 1181 of the bindings — reaches eval_impl and does all the scheduling described above. A neural network is the same story with syntax sugar: mlx.nn layers are dict subclasses that collect parameters recursively, and a forward pass just traces mx calls. Drop a mx.compile around a training step or a nn.value_and_grad around a loss and you are using the transformation machinery without leaving Python.

import mlx.core as mx
import mlx.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 8), nn.relu, nn.Linear(8, 1))
x = mx.random.normal((2, 4))
y = model(x)         # still lazy
mx.eval(y)

Honest Limits

Read the source and the boundaries are clearly marked. First, platform: the Metal backend requires Apple silicon; on Linux the same code compiles against CPU only, and the newly landed CUDA backend under mlx/backend/cuda/ is real but younger and less battle-tested than the Metal path. There is no Windows build. Second, distribution: mlx.distributed exists with MPI and a ring backend, but there is nothing like the tensor-parallel machinery of full serving stacks — MLX targets one machine with a big unified-memory GPU, which is why it pairs so well with single-node model ports rather than vLLM-style cluster serving. Third, operator coverage: the op catalogue is broad but not NumPy-complete, and a few long-tail ops fall back to slower composed paths. Fourth, the Python object model leaks a little — nn.Module is a dict subclass, which makes attribute plumbing occasionally surprising — and compiled functions must be pure, since the compile cache assumes the graph only depends on its inputs. None of these are hidden; they are all visible in the tree we just walked, and that legibility is arguably MLX’s best feature.
entry.summary: Inside Apple's MLX: how ops build a computation graph, how every primitive promises eval_cpu and eval_gpu, how lazy evaluation and a per-stream scheduler interleave CPU and Metal work, and what mlx.nn adds on top.

entry.title: NCNN Source Tour: The Mobile-First C++ Inference Framework

link.title: NCNN Source Tour: The Mobile-First C++ Inference Framework

entry.content:
Most inference frameworks we have toured on this blog — ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, TVM — are desktop-first projects that were later coaxed onto phones. Tencent’s ncnn went the other way. It was born in 2017 for QQ and WeChat-style mobile workloads, written in C++03-friendly C++ with zero third-party dependencies, and it treats an Android phone’s octa-core ARM CPU as the primary target, with Vulkan GPUs as the optional fast path. If llama.cpp is the story of squeezing LLMs out of laptops, ncnn is the story of squeezing convnets into 2 GB of phone RAM in 20 milliseconds a frame.

The design bet is easy to state and easy to miss in the code: no dynamic allocation after warm-up, no hidden OS calls, no abstraction you cannot delete. The whole library is a graph of Layer objects that shuffle refcounted Mat tensors around, and every millisecond-critical kernel has hand-written NEON, AVX, and shader variants. In this tour we read the source the way its authors layered it: the Net and Extractor lifecycle, the two-file model format, the generated layer registry, the big.LITTLE threading story, and the Vulkan detour.

We have covered the training-side tooling before — PyTorch, JAX, MLX — and the serving side in pieces on vLLM and Triton Inference Server. ncnn occupies the opposite corner of that map: no Python at runtime, no server, one .param text file and one .bin weight file shipped inside your APK. Understanding how those two files become matrix multiplies is the whole point of this post.

Overview of ncnn: the Net/Extractor API, the Blob and Mat tensor model, the generated layer registry feeding per-ISA CPU backends and the Vulkan path, plus the PNNX converter that produces the model files.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Net::load_param, L63 parses the text .param file and builds the layer and blob arrays; load_model, L68 fills in weights from the binary .bin.
  • Net::create_extractor, L134 hands out an Extractor, and Extractor::extract, L220 lazily executes only the subgraph your requested output actually needs.
  • Blob, L24 is just a producer and consumer layer index — the DAG is encoded in two ints per edge.
  • Mat::elempack, L360 is the packing factor (1, 4, or 8 floats per SIMD lane group) that every kernel negotiates around.
  • layer_registry_entry, L147 pairs each of ~80 layer types with a creator function; the tables themselves are generated per ISA.
  • create_layer_cpu, L442 picks avx512, avx, rvv, msa, or plain C++ tables at runtime depending on the CPU it lands on.
  • Convolution_arm winograd dispatch, L491 shows the per-shape kernel selection that makes ARM convolution fast.
  • set_cpu_powersave, L3086 pins worker threads to the big or little cluster — a knob almost no desktop framework has.

Two Files, One Model

ncnn models ship as a pair. The .param file starts with the magic number 7767517 — checked at net.cpp L1546 — followed by a layer count, a blob count, and then one line per layer: an index-free row of type, name, input blob count, output blob count, and key=value parameters. Every row is parsed through ParamDict, a small typed key-value store whose getters (paramdict.h L37) return caller-supplied defaults for missing keys, which is how a single Convolution row survives format evolution across a decade.

Weights live in .bin, decoded by ModelBinFromDataReader::load at modelbin.cpp L82. Each weight block begins with a 32-bit flag that names its storage: 0x01306B47 marks fp16 pairs, 0x0002C056 marks quantized int8, and plain float32 blocks carry no flag at all. Because a DataReader abstracts the source (datareader.h L21), the same bytes can stream from a file, a memory buffer, or an Android asset without the layer code caring.

The tooling in tools/ keeps this format honest. pnnx.cpp, L287 drives PNNX, the PyTorch Neural Network Exchange converter that traces TorchScript graphs (far more faithfully than the retired ONNX export path — compare with our ONNX tour) and emits .param/.bin. ncnnoptimize, L2780 folds constants and batch norms, ncnn2mem, L481 packs the pair into C arrays for load_param(const unsigned char*)-style zero-IO loading, and the quantize folder’s ncnn2table, L2310 runs KL-divergence calibration to produce the thresholds ncnn2int8, L1098 needs to rewrite weights.

The Registry: One Class, Nine ISA Tables

The whole kernel story hangs off a single abstract base class. Layer (layer.h L20) declares load_param and load_model for its share of the two files, plus two inference entry points: forward (L95) for the general case and forward_inplace (L100) for layers that can reuse their input buffer. Two capability flags drive the scheduler: one_blob_only (L46) lets the runtime skip vector plumbing for single-input layers, and support_inplace (L49) is what makes ReLU-shaped ops nearly free.

What makes ncnn unusual is how implementations attach. CMake globs src/layer/arm/*.cpp, src/layer/x86/*.cpp, and so on, and stamps out parallel creator tables into layer_registry.h.in (L5): one per CPU ISA plus a Vulkan table. At load time, create_layer (layer.cpp L408) allocates the plain-C++ version and, if the net was built with Vulkan enabled, attaches a GPU twin to the same object. At runtime with NCNN_RUNTIME_CPU enabled, create_layer_cpu (L442) consults the detected ISA and swaps in the avx512 or rvv table — one binary, many CPUs, no dispatch in the hot loop. Registering your own layer type is one register_custom_layer call, with CustomBit (layer_type.h L13) keeping custom indices clear of the built-ins.

Look inside the ARM convolution implementation and the value of that structure shows. The layer’s setup pass at convolution_arm.cpp L117 pre-packs weights into the exact blocked layout its kernels consume; the forward pass at L324 then chooses between transformed-weight Winograd tiles (L491), an im2col+GEMM path (L562), and direct NEON loops by shape. The x86 sibling (convolution_x86.cpp L279) mirrors the same decisions for AVX and AVX512 packs. This is the same “unpack once, run many” philosophy behind GGML’s quantized kernels and CUTLASS’s tiled GEMMs, just aimed at 1x1 and 3x3 convolutions instead of attention.

Threads, Affinity, and the Big.LITTLE Bet

ncnn’s concurrency model is refreshingly blunt: OpenMP. Option::num_threads (option.h L38) is threaded down through every forward call, and kernels carve channels into _nT slices. The interesting part is what surrounds it. cpu.cpp probes the SoC into little, big, and all-cluster affinity masks, and set_cpu_powersave (L3086) moves the process onto one of them; get_big_cpu_count (L3037) then reports how many workers are actually worth spawning. On a phone where the little cores are 4x slower, running 8 threads across all cores is a latency loss — ncnn is one of the few frameworks that encodes that truth in an API.

Memory gets the same treatment. Blobs between layers are refcounted Mats (mat.h L347) — a data pointer, dims w/h/d/c, per-element packing in elempack, and padded channel stride cstep (L373). In light mode the Extractor recycles intermediates through a PoolAllocator (allocator.h L151), so steady-state inference performs no allocation churn, which matters both for latency spikes and for Android’s memory watchdog. Preprocessing lives beside the tensor type: Mat::from_pixels (mat_pixel.cpp L2429) converts NV21 camera frames straight into float tensors, and substract_mean_normalize (mat.cpp L1804) does mean-subtract and scale in one pass.

From Install to Your First Model

Building is a two-line CMake exercise: configure with -DNCNN_VULKAN=ON (or the Android NDK toolchain file) and install; there are no dependencies to hunt beyond OpenMP. The public API then fits on a postcard:

#include "net.h"

ncnn::Net net;
net.opt.num_threads = 4;          // Option knobs, see option.h L38
net.load_param("model.param");    // net.h L75
net.load_model("model.bin");      // net.h L95

ncnn::Mat in = ncnn::Mat::from_pixels(
    rgba_data, ncnn::Mat::PIXEL_RGBA2RGB, 224, 224);
const float mean[3] = {127.5f, 127.5f, 127.5f};
const float norm[3] = {0.007843f, 0.007843f, 0.007843f};
in.substract_mean_normalize(mean, norm);

ncnn::Extractor ex = net.create_extractor();  // net.h L134
ex.input("data", in);                         // net.h L214
ncnn::Mat out;
ex.extract("prob", out);                      // net.h L220

Three things are worth noticing. First, Extractor::extract is pull-based: it walks backwards from the named output through Blob::consumer/producer links and runs only the layers your output depends on, via the recursive forward_layer at net.cpp L138. Second, the same Net can serve many extractors concurrently; blob storage is per-extractor, weights are shared. Third, the error path is honest — extract a misspelled blob name and the runtime logs the exact ex.extract("name", out); lines you should have written, as the lookup failure branch in net.cpp L3194 shows. For a deeper contrast in execution models, see our tour of torch.compile’s runtime and of ExecuTorch, PyTorch’s own answer to on-device.

The Vulkan Detour

When a phone GPU is worth using, ncnn uses it — but on its own terms. Everything is compute-shader based: VkMat (mat.h L389) mirrors Mat with device-memory allocators, and VkCompute (command.h L22) is a reusable command buffer that layers record shader dispatches into. The Vulkan convolution twin sets up its shader bindings and weight staging at convolution_vulkan.cpp L71, and its GPU forward at L1759 records work for the whole graph to submit in one go — ncnn prefers fewer, larger submissions because phone driver overhead dwarfs desktop. Device capability probing (get_gpu_count, gpu.h L185) happens early, and the code is disarmingly pragmatic: at net.cpp L1579, any missing feature quietly flips use_vulkan_compute off and falls back to CPU mid-load. A net can even interleave — the GPU branch of forward_layer (L213) hops between CPU and GPU blobs per layer, staging through host memory when a layer has no shader.

Honest Limits

ncnn is an inference engine with strong opinions, and the edges show. There is no autograd and no training path — unlike tinygrad or PyTorch itself, every graph is frozen at conversion time, and dynamic control flow or data-dependent shapes must be flattened into the static layer list before deployment. The C++-only runtime API is a feature for APK size and a tax for experimentation; the Python bindings exist but are thin, so interactive debugging leans on the benchmark and squeezenet example tools rather than a REPL. Quantization is post-training only and needs a calibration dataset through ncnn2table; there is no QAT story, and quantized accuracy on depthwise-heavy mobile backbones needs the usual per-layer sensitivity massaging. LLM support is real but young: the Extractor grew kv-cache allocators (net.h L195) and the quantize folder gained LLM-specific tables recently, yet the ecosystem of ready-made transformer models is far thinner than llama.cpp’s or MLC-LLM’s. And the layer registry, for all its ISA tables, still expects you to write a shader or NEON intrinsics for any op the converters cannot decompose — extensibility by C++, not by config.

Those limits are the price of the pitch: a 1 MB library, no dependencies, deterministic latency, and kernels you can actually read. For on-device vision work — detection, segmentation, super-resolution, face chains at 60 fps — ncnn remains the reference point every mobile-first runtime is measured against, and its source is one of the best places to learn what “mobile-first” actually costs.
entry.summary: Inside Tencent's ncnn: the Net and Mat lifecycle, the ISA-layered layer registry, big.LITTLE threading, the Vulkan path, and the two-file model format.

entry.title: Outlines Source Tour: Compiling JSON Schemas into Logit Masks

link.title: Outlines Source Tour: Compiling JSON Schemas into Logit Masks

entry.content:
Ask a language model for JSON and it will happily hand you a stray brace, a trailing comma, or a confidently hallucinated field name. Structured generation attacks the problem at the root: instead of parsing and repairing whatever the model emits, you forbid invalid tokens before they are ever sampled. Outlines, maintained by dottxt, is the library that popularized this technique, and its fingerprints are all over modern serving stacks — the guided-decoding paths in vLLM, SGLang, and TGI all grew out of ideas this project proved out in production.

The current main branch of the repository is a good moment to read the source, because the codebase has been deliberately split in two. The pure-Python package under src/outlines handles everything users touch: output types, model wrappers, prompt templates, and the Generator factory. The hot path — compiling a regex against a tokenizer’s vocabulary and walking the resulting finite-state machine token by token — lives in a separate Rust-backed companion package called outlines-core, pinned to version 0.2.14 right in the project’s pyproject.toml. The Python side talks to it through a thin, well-documented boundary.

The whole architecture follows from one observation: whether a token is legal depends on which tokens came before it, and that dependency is exactly what a finite-state machine encodes. So a Python type or JSON schema becomes a Term, the Term becomes a regex, the regex plus the vocabulary of your tokenizer becomes an index over token IDs, and the index drives a per-step bitmask over the logits. Every file in the repository exists to serve one of those five stages. If you have read our tour of transformers, you will recognize the integration point immediately: a logits_processor callback handed to the model’s generate loop.

Overview of the Outlines architecture: the public API compiles output types through the Term DSL, the backend registry delegates to outlines-core or llguidance, and the resulting logits processors are wired into steerable model wrappers that mask logits at every decode step.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Generator factory, L347 is the front door. It inspects the model and returns a SteerableGenerator, a BlackBoxGenerator, or an async variant, depending on whether Outlines controls decoding or merely forwards the output type to a hosted provider.
  • Inside the steerable path, SteerableGenerator.init, L237 normalizes whatever you passed via python_types_to_terms, L730 — dataclasses, TypedDicts, pydantic models, enums, literals, or bare Python values all become Term instances.
  • The term is lowered to a regex by to_regex, L978, which is where a pydantic model becomes a deterministic pattern over token strings rather than a hopeful prompt suffix.
  • The compiled regex is handed to get_json_schema_logits_processor, L58 and its regex and CFG siblings, which route to a backend by name. The defaults live three lines up: JSON_SCHEMA_DEFAULT_BACKEND, L28 is outlines_core, while context-free grammars default to llguidance.
  • The default backend, OutlinesCoreBackend, L176, extracts your tokenizer’s vocabulary, drops the EOS token from it, and compiles Index(regex, self.vocabulary), L250 inside the Rust core.
  • At generation time, OutlinesCoreLogitsProcessor.process_logits, L140 advances one Guide per batch row with the last sampled token and fills a token bitmask before scores are computed.
  • All of that machinery inherits from OutlinesLogitsProcessor, L14, the small base class that standardizes input_ids and logits to 2D tensors and picks the right tensor adapter.
  • On the model side, Transformers, L172 is the canonical steerable wrapper: its generate passes the processor straight into the Hugging Face generate call, while SteerableModel, L32 defines exactly which wrappers qualify.

From Types to Regex: the Term DSL

The most elegant file in the repository is src/outlines/types/dsl.py. It opens with a base Term class, L82 that overloads + and | so that regular-expression composition reads like arithmetic: Regex("[0-9]{4}") + "-" + Regex("[0-9]{2}") builds a Sequence, and either("yes", "no") builds Alternatives. On top of that sit the concrete terms — Regex, L222 for raw patterns, CFG, L241 for context-free grammars loaded from bundled Lark files, and JsonSchema, L282 for schema strings or pydantic models.

The converter that makes this feel magical is python_types_to_terms, L730. An int maps to an integer pattern, a Literal["Positive", "Negative"] maps to alternatives of escaped strings, a plain dict maps to CFG(grammars.json), and dataclasses, TypedDicts, and pydantic models are serialized to JSON schema and then translated to regex by the Rust core’s build_regex_from_schema. There is a recursion guard capped at depth ten, which is a pragmatic admission that recursive schemas will otherwise explode. The pydantic integration is bidirectional: Term.__get_pydantic_json_schema__ at L139 emits a "pattern" keyword, so custom regex types validate inside ordinary pydantic models too.

The Rust Core: Vocabulary, Index, Guide

Three Rust types do the heavy lifting, and the Python adapter around them is refreshingly honest about its job. create_outlines_core_vocabulary, L259 walks your tokenizer’s token -> id mapping, converts each token to its true string representation (so the BPE artifacts like Ġworld become " world"), groups IDs by string, and removes the EOS token — the core adds termination back on its own terms. A regex plus that vocabulary yields an Index, a finite-state machine whose states are sets of token sets; a Guide is a cursor moving through that index as tokens are sampled.

The per-step loop in process_logits is where correctness nuances live. Each batch element’s guide is advanced with the last sampled token id, but only when the guide is unfinished or still accepts the token — the code even cites outlines-core issue 227 as the reason for the workaround at L168. Bitmask allocation and application are delegated to per-library kernels exported by the core, so the hot loops stay in Rust and the Python layer stays thin. This is the same philosophy behind libraries like MLX keeping graph execution native: spend Python only on decisions, not on per-token arithmetic.

One Processor, Three Tensor Libraries

Every logits processor is tensor-library agnostic by construction. The base class selects an adapter from the registry in src/outlines/processors/tensor_adapters/__init__.py — TorchTensorAdapter, L6 for PyTorch, plus numpy and MLX implementations behind the same small protocol of shape, unsqueeze, concatenate, and device moves. When the first token is generated, the processor lazily builds one guide and one bitmask per batch row, choosing the kernel module that matches the library. For torch, bias_logits, L104 fills the bitmask on CPU, ships it to the device holding the logits, applies it in place, and ships it back — a deliberate trade of a couple of transfers per step for a single kernel implementation.

The lazy _setup is a subtle design win: batch size and vocabulary size are unknown until real tensors arrive, so the processor defers all allocation to the first call and then reuses the guides, resetting only the cursor between generations. That is also why the Generator resets its processor at the top of __call__, batch, and stream — reuse the expensive FSM, rewind the cheap state.

Black-Box Models and Provider Routing

Not every model hands you its logits. For hosted providers, Outlines draws a hard line with two protocol unions in src/outlines/models/__init__.py: steerable models (transformers, llama.cpp, L244, MLX-LM, L102) accept logits processors, while black-box models — OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Ollama, and the vLLM server client — receive the raw output type and decide enforcement themselves, usually via structured-output request fields. The BlackBoxGenerator, L28 simply forwards the type, which keeps the same model(prompt, output_type) ergonomics everywhere. For in-process serving there is VLLMOffline, L103 with from_vllm_offline, L278, which converts types with the same DSL and lets the vLLM engine apply masking internally. Provider errors are funneled through normalize_provider_errors into a uniform APIError hierarchy, so your retry logic does not need to know five SDK conventions.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above reduces to a short, verified recipe. Install the library with the transformers extra:

pip install outlines
pip install "outlines[transformers]"

Then wire up any Hugging Face causal LM and constrain it. Both snippets below use only APIs present in the source we just read:

import outlines
from typing import Literal
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model = outlines.from_transformers(
    AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"),
    AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"),
)

# Direct call: the output type is compiled on the fly.
sentiment = model(
    "Analyze: 'This product completely changed my life!'",
    Literal["Positive", "Negative", "Neutral"],
)
print(sentiment)  # exactly one of the three literals

For anything reused, build a Generator once so the FSM is compiled a single time, and validate with pydantic afterwards:

from pydantic import BaseModel

class ProductReview(BaseModel):
    rating: int
    pros: list[str]
    cons: list[str]
    summary: str

generator = outlines.Generator(model, ProductReview)
review = generator("Review: great battery life, runs hot", max_new_tokens=200)
parsed = ProductReview.model_validate_json(review)

The second form matters more than it looks: the generator holds the compiled index, so a loop over ten thousand reviews pays for compilation once. Compiled artifacts are additionally memoized on disk through get_cache, L43, which you can disable or clear via disable_cache and clear_cache. If you prefer prompt-as-function ergonomics, Template, L59 turns annotated Python functions into Jinja prompt builders, and Application, L14 binds a template plus an output type into a callable.

Honest Limits

Context-free grammars are the sharpest edge. The default JSON-schema and regex backends cannot handle them at all — the outlines-core backend raises NotImplementedError for CFGs at L253 — so grammatical outputs ride entirely on llguidance, and a plain dict output type inherits that route too. Streaming is not implemented for transformers models; generate_stream raises NotImplementedError at L355, pending upstream support in the Hugging Face generate loop. The Rust-backed processor also supports only three tokenizer extraction paths — transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX — so exotic steerable models cannot use the default backend until someone writes the vocabulary shim.

Two more caveats belong in any honest review. First, the JAX and TensorFlow model paths emit deprecation warnings in the source and explicitly do not support structured generation, so PyTorch is the practical target. Second, for black-box providers Outlines cannot guarantee anything: it serializes your schema into the request and trusts the provider’s enforcement, which varies. None of this diminishes the core achievement. The repository demonstrates, file by file, that the gap between “the model usually returns valid JSON” and “the model cannot return anything else” is a compiler problem — and one that a few thousand lines of Python plus a Rust core can close completely.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the dottxt-ai/outlines codebase: the Term DSL, outlines-core's Rust-backed Index and Vocabulary, pluggable constraint backends, and tensor-agnostic logit masking.

entry.title: PyTorch Source Tour: One Op Call from Python to the Caching Allocator

link.title: PyTorch Source Tour: One Op Call from Python to the Caching Allocator

entry.content:
Almost every framework we have toured on this blog sits on the same substrate. vLLM [(/vllm-2/)] spends its effort on KV-cache management and batch scheduling, but its tensor math is PyTorch. TorchServe [(/torchserve/)] and ExecuTorch [(/executorch/)] exist to package and run models that were defined and trained in PyTorch in the first place. Even compact educational engines like nanoGPT [(/nanogpt/)] are best understood as deliberate shrinks of what PyTorch does. So it is worth opening the box itself: the pytorch/pytorch repository is one of the most instructive C++ codebases in open source, and its layering explains much of the behavior you observe from Python every day.

This tour follows a single op call from the very top to the very bottom. You write y = model(x) and loss.backward() in Python; we will end at a CUDA kernel writing its results into memory that was carved out of a cached block pool by the caching allocator. Between those two points sit five distinct layers: the Python module machinery, the operator registry, the C++ dispatcher, the autograd engine, and the backend kernels with their memory management. Each layer has a clean job, and each one is independently interesting.

A note on method: every file link below points at a specific line in the pytorch/pytorch repository on the main branch, and every line number was verified against a fresh checkout while writing this. Line numbers drift on a codebase this active, but the symbols are stable; if a link lands a line or two off, search for the symbol name in the same file.

The overview map: a Python nn.Module call descends through the dispatcher into the autograd engine, backend kernels, and finally the CUDA caching allocator, while the optimizer closes the loop back to the weights.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • _wrapped_call_impl, L1783 and _call_impl, L1791: the Python entry point where forward hooks run before your own forward method is invoked.
  • Parameter, L30: a torch.Tensor subclass whose requires_grad flag defaults to True, so every weight a module owns is automatically tracked.
  • native_functions.yaml, L1: the declarative registry where every aten operator is named and typed before code generation turns it into C++ and Python bindings.
  • Dispatcher::findSchemaOrThrow, L150 and TypedOperatorHandle::call, L623: how a call by name becomes a typed C++ fast path.
  • TensorImpl.key_set_, L650 and DispatchKeySet, L167: the bitset on every tensor that decides whether a call goes to autograd first and then to a concrete backend.
  • autograd Node, L130 and Engine::execute, L1428: the recorded graph and the engine that replays it on backward.
  • CPU mul_kernel, L126 and CUDA mul_kernel_cuda, L22: the same operator, two concrete kernels behind one dispatch table.
  • CUDACachingAllocator malloc, L1846: where the output tensor’s GPU storage actually comes from.

One Call, Five Layers

Take the simplest possible training step: a linear layer applied to a batch, then a loss. On the Python side, model(x) does not call your forward method directly. The class attribute __call__ is bound to _wrapped_call_impl at module.py L1926, which forwards into _call_impl at L1791. That is where hooks live: global and per-module forward hooks are wrapped so they can see the owning module, a job done by _WrappedHook, whose call, L85 injects the module reference before delegating to the user’s hook. Only after the hook machinery does your forward run, and for a linear layer it ends in F.linear, which calls the C++ operator aten::addmm.

Now the C++ side takes over, and the fast path is worth reading slowly. The typed template Dispatcher::call begins at Dispatcher.h L784: it asks the handle’s dispatchKeyExtractor, L505 to compute a key set from the tensor arguments, then looks up the matching kernel and invokes it. If the arguments require gradient, the autograd key is in the set, so the call first lands in an autograd kernel, which records what happened and then redispatches to the real backend kernel. The result flows back up to Python as an ordinary tensor that quietly carries a gradient function with it.

The detail map: the dispatcher's typed call path, the tensor-side key set, the engine's queue-and-drain loop, and the two backend kernels that share a TensorIterator-style interface.

Inside the Dispatcher

The dispatcher is the reason PyTorch can support autograd, tracing, functional transforms, and half a dozen hardware backends without turning every operator function into spaghetti. The design starts from native_functions.yaml, L1, a declarative file listing every operator’s name, signature, and where its implementations live. Code generation reads it and produces the bindings you use from Python and C++.

At runtime each operator is represented by an OperatorEntry, L70, which holds a table mapping dispatch keys to registered kernels. The same aten::mul name can simultaneously have an autograd wrapper, a composite implementation, a CPU kernel, and a CUDA kernel registered under different keys. Choosing among them happens through key sets: DispatchKeyExtractor, L128 knows which arguments matter, and its getDispatchKeySetUnboxed, L194 ORs the key sets of all tensor arguments into one bitset. That bitset is built from BackendComponent, L65 values, an enum of CPU, CUDA, and other backends packed as bit positions, and wrapped in the DispatchKeySet, L167 class every TensorImpl carries.

This is also the extension point for the wider ecosystem. Custom CUDA libraries like FlashAttention [(/flash-attention/)] and Triton [(/triton/)] kernels can be registered as first-class operators through torch.library, at which point they ride the exact same path as built-ins. Serving frameworks like vLLM [(/vllm-2/)] use the same mechanism to register fused attention and sampling ops that the dispatcher cannot distinguish from native ones.

The Autograd Engine

Forward execution records; backward execution computes. Every differentiable op contributes an autograd Node, L130, which stores the edges to its consumers and an apply function that computes one backward step. When you call loss.backward(), the engine takes over at Engine::execute, L1428. It first runs compute_dependencies, L1360 (invoked at L1494) to count how many gradient contributions each node is waiting for, then pushes ready nodes into per-device queues. Those queues are the device_ready_queues_, L246 members of the Engine struct, L131, one worker thread per device.

From there the loop is thread_main, L575: pop a node, accumulate its incoming gradients into an InputBuffer, L41, call the node’s apply, and push whatever becomes ready. Gradients arriving through several branches are summed in the buffer before the node fires, which is exactly the semantics you want from a fork-join graph. When the last node finishes, exec_post_processing, L765 synchronizes per-device streams and runs final callbacks.

This engine is why distributed trainers can hook in cleanly. DeepSpeed [(/deepspeed/)] and Accelerate [(/accelerate/)] wrap the standard step with gradient accumulation hooks, gradient clipping, and all-reduce calls, but the underlying graph walk is the one described above. And once gradients have landed on each Parameter’s .grad field, Adam.step, L216 consumes them, expressing its elementwise updates as ordinary dispatched tensor ops, including fused foreach variants that batch many parameters into fewer kernel launches.

Kernels and Memory

Below autograd sits the code that actually multiplies numbers. Binary elementwise ops converge on TensorIteratorBase, L246, which normalizes shapes and strides, handles broadcasting, picks a common dtype, and decides the loop structure. On top of it, the CPU mul_kernel, L126 runs vectorized inner loops selected per scalar type, while the CUDA mul_kernel_cuda, L22 hands an elementwise functor to a GPU launch helper. Two files, one contract: that contract is what makes an operator portable.

Memory is the last layer and a quietly important one. Calling cudaMalloc for every activation would dominate latency, so the CUDACachingAllocator, L1846 malloc instead splits, rounds, and recycles cached blocks that are stream-aware: a block freed on one stream is only reused where it is safe. This caching behavior is why GPU memory in PyTorch looks “stuck” at a high watermark after a big batch, and why torch.cuda.empty_cache() exists as an escape hatch. Projects like CUTLASS [(/cutlass/)] plug in below this line, providing the tile-level GEMM primitives that the highest-performance kernels call into.

From Install to Your First Model

The easiest way to get all of this running is the official wheel. For a CPU-only setup, pip install torch is enough; for a CUDA build, pick the wheel index matching your toolkit:

pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124

Then a complete training loop, small enough to read and large enough to touch every layer of this tour:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(784, 128),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(128, 10),
)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for step in range(10):
    x = torch.randn(64, 784)
    y = torch.randint(0, 10, (64,))
    pred = model(x)          # __call__ -> hooks -> forward -> aten ops
    loss = loss_fn(pred, y)  # dispatcher records an autograd graph
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()          # Engine::execute walks the recorded graph
    opt.step()               # Adam.step updates every Parameter

Each line maps to a layer from the diagrams: model(x) enters through _call_impl, the arithmetic dispatches through OperatorEntry tables into CPU or CUDA kernels, loss.backward() hands the recorded nodes to the engine and its per-device queues, and opt.step() runs the update math through the dispatcher again. If you want to appreciate how much engineering hides in those lines, try nanoGPT [(/nanogpt/)] or tinygrad [(/tinygrad/)], where the same concepts are implemented in a few thousand lines instead of a few hundred thousand.

Honest Limits

A tour like this compresses, so here is what it leaves out. Building PyTorch from source is a serious undertaking: CMake-driven, with dozens of optional dependencies, and a compile time measured in tens of minutes to hours depending on your machine. The build system and the code generators under tools/ that turn native_functions.yaml into thousands of lines of glue are a project of their own and were skipped entirely. Also skipped: torch.compile and its Inductor code generator, the functorch and vmap transforms that layer above the dispatcher, the distributed c10d stack, and the newer backends for MPS and other accelerators.

The dispatcher itself has a genuine learning curve. Dispatch keys, include and exclude sets, thread-local state, and the boxed versus unboxed calling conventions interact in ways that only make sense after a few debugging sessions; the tour presented the happy path where autograd wraps and redispatches, but real traces show fallthroughs, aliases, and special cases. The diagrams simplify deliberately: an inference-mode tensor skips autograd entirely, and a compiled graph may never touch the dispatcher for fused regions at all. Finally, remember that line numbers in a repository this active move weekly; treat every deep link here as a snapshot of a moving target, and use the symbol names as the durable handle.
entry.summary: Follow one tensor operation end to end through nn.Module, the C++ dispatcher, the autograd engine, CPU and CUDA kernels, and the CUDA caching allocator, with line-level links into pytorch/pytorch.

entry.title: Safetensors Source Tour: The Zero-Copy Weight Container

link.title: Safetensors Source Tour: The Zero-Copy Weight Container

entry.content:
Every large model you download today is, on disk, mostly just a bag of numbers. The interesting engineering question is what wraps around that bag. For years the answer in the PyTorch world was torch.save, which wraps Python pickle — arbitrary code execution on load, no partial loading, no framework neutrality. Safetensors is Hugging Face’s answer: a tiny, deliberately boring container format that stores tensors as raw bytes preceded by a small JSON header, with serialization and deserialization implemented once in a dependency-light Rust core and exposed to Python, plus ports for numpy, JAX, TensorFlow, Paddle and MLX. If you have read our tokenizers source tour, the shape of the project will feel familiar: a compact Rust crate, a PyO3 binding layer, and thin per-framework Python modules on top.

The design bet is that a checkpoint should be mmap-able: the loader should not have to read, copy or even deserialize tensor bytes to put them where a framework wants them. That single bet explains almost everything in the codebase — the 8-byte header preamble, the strict offset validation, the torch.UntypedStorage trick, the pread(2) backend, and the DLPack hand-off for CUDA and Metal. It is also why serving stacks like vLLM, TGI and the Transformers library made safetensors the default weight format; fast weight streaming is a load-time problem, and safetensors attacks it at the file-format level rather than with application-side tricks.

This post tours the actual source: the format contract, the Rust validation core, the zero-copy paths, the async prefetch engine, and the per-framework ports. As usual, every linked symbol below points at the exact line on main at the time of writing, so you can follow along in the repository.

Overview of safetensors: a no_std Rust core parses and validates the header, the PyO3 binding layer exposes safe_open with mmap/pread backends and a background prefetch engine, and pure-Python ports adapt the result to torch, numpy, JAX and friends.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The format contract is documented in the crate README: 8 bytes: N, L76 — an unsigned little-endian 64-bit integer giving the size of the JSON header, followed by N bytes of header and then the raw tensor bytes.
  • MAX_HEADER_SIZE, L10 caps that header at 100,000,000 bytes, which bounds the cost of parsing metadata no matter how many tensors a file declares.
  • read_metadata, L390 reads the u64 length, slices the header bytes, checks UTF-8 and JSON validity, then runs validation before anything is returned.
  • validate, L627 is the security heart: offsets must be contiguous and increasing, and each tensor’s span must exactly equal shape product times dtype bitsize.
  • SafeTensors::deserialize, L446 turns a validated buffer into a SafeTensors whose tensors are borrowed views — zero bytes are copied.
  • safe_open, L1704 is the PyO3 front door: a Python context manager that parses the header once and serves tensors lazily.
  • Storage, L594 enumerates the serving strategies: a plain Rust Mmap, a torch-owned UntypedStorage, a Paddle MmapStorage, or an open file handle for pread.
  • Loader, L755 is the background engine behind safe_open.prefetch: worker threads read planned byte spans into pinned slabs and stage them into CUDA buffers.
  • save_file, L288 is the most-used port API; it flattens tensors to raw pointers and delegates to the Rust serializer.

The 8-Byte Header That Kills Pickle

A safetensors file is N (8 bytes, little-endian) + N bytes of JSON + raw tensor data. The JSON is a dict keyed by tensor name, where each value is a TensorInfo, L799 holding dtype, shape, and data_offsets — a (begin, end) pair into the data section. An optional __metadata__ key carries free-form string annotations. The README states the dict layout precisely at the header grammar, L80.

Two implementation details are worth noticing. First, when writing, the serializer pads the JSON header with spaces to the next multiple of 8 bytes, so the data section starts at an aligned offset; you can see this in serialize, L268 and its file-based sibling serialize_to_file, L348, which streams through a buffered writer and a temp-file rename so existing mmaps never see a truncated file. Second, the Dtype enum, L811 has 22 variants ranging from BOOL and 16-bit floats to FP8 variants and 4-bit F4, each reporting its width through bitsize, L867. Sub-byte dtypes are the reason bitsize exists: a 4-bit tensor’s byte length is no longer n_elements * size_in_bytes, and several APIs had to grow bitsize-aware arithmetic.

Compared with pickle-based checkpoints, this header buys three concrete properties: loading is language-neutral (the format is trivially parseable in C, Rust, Go or JavaScript), loading is partial (you can mmap the file, read one tensor’s span, and touch nothing else), and loading is safe (the header cannot contain code). The Transformers docs and our PyTorch tour cover the migration story from .bin files; here we care about how the container enforces its own safety.

Validation Before a Single Byte Moves

The Rust core treats every input as hostile. The SafeTensorError enum, L16 lists the failure modes: header too small, header too large, invalid UTF-8, invalid JSON, invalid header length, tensor not found, invalid offsets, and incomplete buffer coverage.
