The parse path in read_metadata uses checked arithmetic throughout — checked_add on the header end, try_into on the u64 length — so a malformed length cannot wrap around into a bogus slice.

The deepest check is Metadata::validate, L627. It walks tensors in offset order and requires that each tensor starts exactly where the previous one ended, that end >= start, that the element count times bitsize (computed with checked_mul) matches the declared span, and it returns the final offset so the caller can confirm the header plus data exactly covers the file. If the last tensor’s end does not land on the buffer end, deserialization fails with MetadataIncompleteBuffer. This is what makes the zero-copy guarantee sound: a view handed to a framework can never point outside the file, overlap a neighbor, or disagree with its declared shape.

The JSON itself is parsed into HashMetadata, L540, a serde helper with __metadata__ skipped when absent and tensor entries flattened into a map, then converted into the ordered Metadata struct at Metadata, L532. The repo also carries an attacks/ directory full of adversarial scripts (DoS-style giant tensors, aliasing tricks against torch and TF loaders), and a fuzz target at fuzz_target!, L6 that feeds random bytes to deserialize — validation is not an afterthought here, it is the product.

The Zero-Copy Path: mmap, UntypedStorage, pread

Opening a file through safe_open constructs an Open, L752 state object that picks one of the strategies in the Backend enum, L402: mmap (map the file copy-on-read and serve views into it) or pread (keep the handle open and read exact byte ranges on demand). The Framework enum, L436 and Device enum, L487 are parsed from Python strings like "pt", "cuda:0", "mps" via parse_device, L520, and the cross product decides what “zero-copy” means:

  • numpy-style frameworks get a view of the mmap handed to np.frombuffer-style construction, zero copies.
  • PyTorch (1.11+) gets the best path: the file is re-opened through torch.UntypedStorage.from_file, so the mmap is owned by torch itself, and each tensor is a torch.asarray(...).view(dtype) over a byte slice of that storage — the returned tensor literally aliases the file’s page cache.
  • Paddle 3.1.1+ mirrors that with paddle.MmapStorage.
  • For CUDA/MPS destinations, bytes must move, and the code moves them with intent: parallel_pread, L2377 reads ranges concurrently via read_exact_at, L2343, with macOS page-cache bypass via disable_page_cache_macos, L2321.

The prefetch engine generalizes the direct-to-GPU idea. safe_open.prefetch(plan) builds a LoadPlan, L200 of disjoint byte Spans, L193, runs worker, L885 threads that chunk reads into pinned staging slabs, and stages results into CudaBuffer, L296 allocations through the hand-rolled driver API in CudaApi, L82. Device buffers then reach Python through DLPack: to_capsule, L233 wraps a DLManagedTensor whose data pointer trait is implemented for CUDA buffers and for shared Metal buffers in MTLBuffer, L61 — the same mechanism Apple’s MLX stack consumes. The result is for name, tensor in loader: yielding ready CUDA tensors while the disk reads continue in the background.

Slicing Without Loading

A lesser-known API makes even partial reads lazy. f.get_slice("name") returns a PySafeSlice, L1908, a handle carrying the tensor’s TensorMeta — dtype, shape, offsets — without touching data. Indexing it invokes __getitem__, L2102, which parses arbitrary Python indexing (ints, slices, ellipsis) via parse_indexers, L307 into Rust TensorIndexer, L58 values, then computes the touched byte ranges with the SliceIterator, L275. For sub-byte dtypes, slice_byte_ranges, L335 handles the alignment puzzles. Only the sliced regions are materialized — useful for sharded inference where you want one row of a giant embedding table. The type stub published to users documents all of this at class safe_open, L213.

From Install to Your First Model

Install the wheel (the Rust extension is prebuilt; the build itself is maturin plus PyO3 configured at the maturin section, L94 and pinned at pyo3 with abi3-py310, L13, one ABI for all Python 3.10+):

pip install safetensors

Round-trip a tensor dict with the torch port, then read it back lazily:

import torch
from safetensors.torch import save_file, load_file
from safetensors import safe_open

tensors = {"weight": torch.randn(512, 1024), "bias": torch.randn(512)}
save_file(tensors, "model.safetensors", metadata={"format": "pt"})

loaded = load_file("model.safetensors")            # zero-copy mmap path

with safe_open("model.safetensors", framework="pt") as f:
    print(f.keys())                                # tensor names from the header
    meta = f.get_tensor_meta("weight")             # dtype/shape/offsets, no data read
    row = f.get_slice("weight")[0, :64]            # lazy slice, only 256 bytes touched

save_file refuses to silently duplicate shared storages; the torch port detects aliased tensors with _find_shared_tensors, L76 and resolves keep-names via _remove_duplicate_names, L97 — the same machinery behind save_model and load_model. The numpy port at save_file, L61 is the reference implementation every other port imitates; JAX, TensorFlow, MLX and Paddle ports are thin numpy bridges (flax, L40, tensorflow, L41, mlx, L41, paddle, L51). For bulk conversion of existing checkpoints, the repo ships convert_file, L216, which rewrites pickle checkpoints in place.

Honest Limits

  • The header is not zero-copy, by the author’s own admission at design notes, L158: JSON is parsed eagerly on open. For a 7B model the header is kilobytes, so this is fine — but a file with millions of tiny tensors pays a real parse cost.
  • The 100MB header cap at MAX_HEADER_SIZE, L10 is a hard ceiling; files with pathological tensor counts cannot be opened at all.
  • No compression, no encryption, no chunked/tiled layout, no checksums. Safetensors is deliberately a dumb container; if you need quantized block layouts or shard manifests you build them above it — GGUF’s approach in the llama.cpp world packs more into the file, at the cost of a much bigger spec.
  • Sub-byte dtypes error out on unaligned operations (MisalignedSlice) rather than silently rounding.
  • Prefetch-to-GPU is Unix-only today; the Windows Loader stub, L54 returns an error, and CUDA staging requires the hand-rolled driver bindings.
  • Saving requires dense, contiguous tensors; sparse or strided views must be materialized first, and concurrent mutation of tensors during save_file can corrupt output (the docstring warns about exactly this).

The takeaway: safetensors wins by being small. Eight bytes of preamble, a validated JSON header, and the discipline to never copy a byte you can alias. That is a good design lesson for anyone building infrastructure around inference runtimes — the fastest code is the load you never do.
entry.summary: How Hugging Face's safetensors stores model weights: an 8-byte header, validated JSON metadata, a no_std Rust core, and zero-copy mmap, pread and DLPack paths through PyO3 into every major framework.

entry.title: Tokenizers Source Tour: The Rust Engine Behind Every HF Tokenizer

link.title: Tokenizers Source Tour: The Rust Engine Behind Every HF Tokenizer

entry.content:
Every request that reaches a large language model is translated twice by the same unglamorous layer: from text into token ids on the way in, and from ids back to text on the way out. When you load a model through Transformers, the component doing that work is huggingface/tokenizers — a Rust library wearing a thin Python skin. It is the first thing your prompt touches and the last thing your generated answer passes through, which makes it one of the most executed pieces of code in the entire inference stack. This post is a source tour of the repository’s main branch as of October 2026, and the timing could not be better: the codebase is mid-rewrite.

The old layout — one big crate with tokenizer/, models/, normalizers/, pre_tokenizers/ folders — is gone. On main the project has been carved into a Cargo workspace of focused crates: tk-encode holds the inference core, tk-serialize is a hand-written reader for tokenizer.json, tk-convert upgrades legacy configs, tk-train hosts the trainers, and a new crate called bitcannon replaces the scalar regex state machines with bit-parallel programs executed 64 bytes at a time. The core object is now deliberately encode-only and read-only: it loads what a tokenizer.json describes and runs it as fast as it can, deferring the build-a-tokenizer-in-code surface to a later release.

Why care about internals? Because tokenization is CPU work on the critical path of every serving stack, including vLLM and SGLang, and because the rewrite is a masterclass in performance engineering under a compatibility contract: byte-exact parity with the previous release, verified against an oniguruma oracle, while every buffer between stages gets fused, pooled or cached. The rest of this post walks through the pieces, with links pinned to verified line numbers so you can follow along in the source.

Overview of the tokenizers workspace on main: the umbrella crate and its JSON reader feed the encode path, which dispatches to four model engines over bitcannon, wrapped by PyO3 bindings and trained from Rust by tk-train.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • the umbrella crate, L79 — tokenizers/src/lib.rs re-exports the workspace crates so existing tokenizers::… import paths keep working.
  • canonicalize_file, L96 — the upgrade pass that rewrites a legacy tokenizer.json into the canonical form the reader accepts.
  • from_json_file, L87 — the hand-written reader that assembles the core tokenizer with no serde anywhere.
  • the BPE model struct, L52 — the fused BPE engine with its atom tables and byte gate.
  • merge_word, L150 — the length-gated dispatcher: short words to multipass, long words to a hot/cold queue.
  • Lattice::viterbi, L176 — Unigram’s dynamic-programming search for the best piece segmentation.
  • WordPiece, L108 — greedy longest-match-first segmentation behind BERT-family models.
  • Whitespace, L56 — a pre-tokenizer implemented directly over bitcannon’s class-run machinery.
  • PyO3 Tokenizer, L22 — the frozen Python class that wraps the Rust core and releases the GIL while encoding.

A Workspace Rebuilt Around One Hot Path

The root crate is now almost entirely documentation and re-exports. Its module list tells you the architecture in one glance: tk_encode for inference, tk_serialize for reading and writing JSON, tk_convert for the legacy-config upgrade pass, and tk_train behind an opt-in feature. The crate docs are unusually honest about scope — they list exactly what the release does not have, and explain that the reader accepts only the canonical config form. That is why tk-convert exists: canonicalize_file normalizes a tokenizer.json written by any older version, and the reader refuses nothing else.

The feature system is worth a minute because it changes how you deploy. Default features cover every model, every Unicode-table normalizer, batch encoding across threads with rayon, and JSON output. Training, Hub downloads and the fancy-regex engine are opt-in. The docs make a promise that only a project with a real test suite would dare: turn the defaults off, keep just features = ["bpe"], and a config that names a component you compiled out fails at load — loudly, not silently. For embedded or edge builds this is a genuine size win.

The Encode Path, Buffer by Buffer

The encode entry accepts a single string, a pair, or a batch, and returns a handle rather than blocking unconditionally — with the parallelism feature, large inputs stream results back as threads finish. One sequence then follows a fixed choreography, every step engineered to avoid allocation:

  1. Special and added tokens are carved out first, in two passes: over the raw input, then again over each segment after normalization, so tokens declared on either form are caught. A segment iterator yields alternating runs of ordinary text and special-token ids.
  2. Each text chunk runs through the normalizer chain — a Cow<str> fold where implementations may return borrowed text when nothing changed. BertNormalizer (clean text, Chinese-char spacing, accent stripping, lowercasing) is the classic example; Metaspace handles sentencepiece-style space encoding.
  3. The normalized chunk is cut into byte ranges, or spans, by a pre-tokenizer. This is the step bitcannon took over: the Whitespace implementation tags each byte with a 16-class atom classifier and cuts on class runs, under an unsafe contract requiring every span to sit on UTF-8 char boundaries.
  4. The model receives the whole span list in one call and appends vocabulary ids into the caller’s output vector. Per-engine scratch buffers are pooled and cleared rather than reallocated, so tokenizing allocates nothing; a per-thread word cache means a repeated word costs one probe instead of a merge loop.
  5. Post-processing joins the pieces: truncation (truncate_pair implements the longest_first, only_first and only_second strategies while respecting the special-token budget), then a template that appends [CLS]/[SEP]-style specials with their type ids. Batch padding (pad_encodings) adds the attention-mask plane.

The output Encoding stores ids as a flat u32 vector with optional type-id and mask planes, and the core marks “all zeros” and “all ones” planes as absent so equality and copies stay cheap. Decode has its own fast path: for byte-level BPE the vocabulary was rewritten at load time into decoded raw bytes, so decoding a sequence of ids is just a concatenation of borrowed slices — no decoder component runs at all. Everything else routes through the configured Decoder trait (decoders/mod.rs, L21), which chains pieces like the WordPiece joiner or the byte-level mapper in reverse.

Four Models, Two Strategies

The model dispatcher — an enum in the same file as the core Model trait — covers BPE, Unigram, WordLevel and WordPiece, each with its own scratch variant so the wrong buffers are unrepresentable. The four engines split into two philosophies.

BPE is the deep one. The engine keeps atoms (raw bytes for byte-level models, chars otherwise), merge tables, and a gate indexed by the word’s first content byte: words shorter than the gate threshold go to a branch-light multipass merger, longer ones to a two-tier hot/cold priority queue (merge_with_queue, L36; the multipass variant lives at merge_multipass.rs, L112). The cleverest trick is prove_fold: at load time the engine walks the vocabulary once and proves, per id, whether a pre-token equal to that entry reproduces itself under merging — one bit per id. A whole-word match can then skip the merge loop entirely, a replacement for the old ignore_merges flag that actually ignores rather than hoping. Scratch state (BpeScratch, L173) carries the symbol vector, queue arenas and an optional WordCache, L65.

Unigram is the probabilistic opposite: instead of greedy merges it builds a lattice over all candidate pieces and searches (Lattice, L53; the model that feeds it sits at Unigram, L21). Viterbi finds the best segmentation by score; the same structure supports n-best lists, posterior sampling for subword regularization, and marginal population for training. WordPiece stays deliberately boring — greedy longest-match-first with the 100-character unk guard (tokenize, L163) — and WordLevel is a straight vocabulary lookup (WordLevel, L78).

bitcannon: Pre-Tokenization as Bitstreams

The most novel crate has a paper behind it. bitcannon follows Interleaved Bitstream Execution for Multi-Pattern Regex Matching on GPUs (MICRO’25) but adapts two portable ideas to a CPU. First, bit-parallel matching: the GPT-family splitting rules compile into character-class bitstreams — one bit per input byte — combined with boolean ops and carry-propagating adds, so 64 input bytes are decided per register operation, branchlessly. Second, interleaving: instead of running one loop per instruction over the whole input (materializing every intermediate stream), all instructions are fused into a single block-wise loop where an intermediate stream lives in a register for its brief lifetime. The only thing that reaches memory is the final starts bitmap.

The crate’s module docs (bitcannon/src/lib.rs, L1) are the best systems-writing in the repo. Supporting machinery includes the SIMD classifier (classify, L134) with AVX2 and NEON paths, and shipped grammars for GPT-2 (bitcannon_byte_level, L16) plus cl100k, o200k, Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi and Tekken. Each grammar is tested byte-exact against an oniguruma oracle across a block-phase sweep — the tests/parity.rs files exist precisely so “faster” never quietly becomes “different”.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one line, plus the Hub helper for downloads:

pip install tokenizers
pip install huggingface_hub   # only needed for from_pretrained

The Python surface is intentionally small — Tokenizer, Encoding, Padding, Truncation. Everything you need for a first run fits on one screen:

from tokenizers import Tokenizer

# From the Hub (delegates the download to huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download)
tok = Tokenizer.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2")

# Or from a local file you already have:
# tok = Tokenizer.from_file("tokenizer.json")

enc = tok.encode("The Rust engine behind every tokenizer.")
print(len(enc))            # number of tokens
print(enc.ids[:8])         # first eight vocabulary ids
print(enc.type_ids)        # [0, 0, ...] for a single sequence

print(tok.tokenize("The Rust engine behind every tokenizer."))
# token strings (byte-level pieces for GPT-2), not ids

print(tok.decode(enc.ids)) # round-trips back to the original text

That is the whole API loop: from_file/from_pretrained load, encode/encode_batch tokenize, decode un-tokenizes. On the rewritten main branch the Encoding object exposes ids, type_ids and attention_mask as lists plus uint32 numpy array variants (the ids getter, L50) — deliberately lean. encode_batch accepts a mix of strings and pairs, and per-call padding/truncation keyword arguments override the config without mutating the tokenizer. Batch encoding releases the GIL while Rust runs, which is why the library threads well inside NumPy-heavy data loaders. And when you eventually serve the model, the ids produced here flow unchanged into runtimes like llama.cpp — tokenization is the contract between training-time text and serving-time ints, which is why byte-exact parity is treated as a hard invariant rather than a nice-to-have.

Honest Limits

  • The object model is deferred. On the rewrite, the Rust-side Tokenizer builder API — constructing a tokenizer in code, add_tokens, save, truncation and padding setters — is explicitly not in this release. The core is read-only: it encodes and decodes what a tokenizer.json describes. Building or editing configs still belongs to released versions or to transformers.
  • The Python Encoding is leaner than it used to be. No offsets, no per-word ids, no token-strings getter. Alignment work (highlighting, mapping spans back to source text) is not served by the new binding yet.
  • Training is Rust-only. The Trainer trait (trainer.rs, L6) and BpeTrainer (BpeTrainer, L214) live behind the train feature; the Python binding in the rewrite has no trainer surface at all.
  • Feature gates are load-time strict. Compile without unigram and a config that references it fails at load. Split/Replace patterns the built-in engines do not cover need the opt-in regex feature (fancy-regex), or the config fails too.
  • bitcannon’s byte-exactness is scoped. It covers the GPT-family grammars it ships, each pinned by parity tests against the oniguruma oracle. Anything outside that set falls back to the classic engines or the regex feature.
  • API drift is real. Serving stacks like TGI pin released versions, and main is explicitly a release-candidate rewrite. Pin your version and check which side of the rewrite your installed wheel is on before writing code against it.
entry.summary: A line-verified source tour of huggingface/tokenizers on main: the workspace rewrite, the encode hot path, BPE, Unigram and WordPiece engines, bitcannon bitstream pre-tokenization, PyO3 bindings and the BpeTrainer.

entry.title: TT-Metal Source Tour: Two Stacks on One RISC-V Accelerator

link.title: TT-Metal Source Tour: Two Stacks on One RISC-V Accelerator

entry.content:
Most inference frameworks we have toured on this blog, like vLLM for serving, llama.cpp for local chat, or PyTorch itself as the universal substrate, sit on top of somebody else’s hardware abstraction. Tenstorrent’s tt-metal is the opposite kind of project: it is the hardware abstraction. It is a single open-source repository that contains the low-level device driver, the dispatch firmware running on RISC-V cores inside the chip, and a full tensor-library front end named ttnn. If you have ever wondered what lives underneath a serving stack, this repo is as deep as it gets without taping out silicon yourself.

The repository organizes that ambition into two clearly separated stacks. The lower one, historically called tt-metalium, lives under tt_metal/ and speaks in the vocabulary of the machine: devices, command queues, buffers, programs, and raw RISC-V kernels. The upper one, ttnn, lives under ttnn/ and speaks in the vocabulary of machine learning: tensors, matmuls, layer norms, and sharded memory configs. Python only ever touches the upper stack, and every Python call bottoms out in C++ that builds a program for the device. This tour walks that path end to end, the same way we walked the compiler story for TVM and the kernel-authoring story for Triton and CUTLASS, but this time the “backend” is a physical card with Tensix cores on it.

We read the main branch, mapped both stacks into two diagrams (an overview and a detail view), and verified every line anchor against the working tree. The single best angle for understanding tt-metal is the seam: what exactly happens between ttnn.matmul(a, b) in Python and a multiply running on a RISC-V core that Python will never see.

Overview: a ttnn call crosses nanobind into C++ operations, which assemble a tt-metalium Program; fast dispatch serializes it into command pages that firmware kernels on the card consume. Files are linked at the anchor lines cited below.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • MatmulDeviceOperation re-export, L25: the Python ttnn.matmul module is thin; the real operation object is imported straight out of the compiled ttnn._ttnn extension.
  • NB_MODULE(_ttnn, mod), L233: the nanobind extension root. It first defines submodules (tensor, device, operations), then binds classes, then binds functions, in that order.
  • Tensor matmul(), L388: the C++ entry point, which normalizes arguments and forwards to the primitive ttnn::prim::matmul.
  • MatmulDeviceOperation::select_program_factory, L2538: the op framework chooses among program factories based on shape, dtype, and the user’s program config.
  • tt_metal::CreateKernel, L634: inside a factory, ttnn stops being a tensor library and becomes a tt-metalium client, attaching reader, mcast, writer, and compute kernels to a Program.
  • class Program, L24: tt-metalium’s unit of work: kernels, circular buffers, and semaphores destined for one device launch.
  • assemble_device_commands, L2417: the dispatcher-to-be serializes the program into CQ commands, runtime-argument writes, and launch messages.
  • class HWCommandQueue, L30: the host-side queue that owns those command pages in system memory.
  • kernel_main, L1589: the on-card dispatcher firmware; it consumes command pages and fires launch messages at worker cores over the NOC.

Two Stacks, One Accelerator

The tt_metal/ tree splits into a public API and an implementation. The API surface is unusually clean for a hardware stack: class IDevice, L64 declares what a device can do (worker cores, sub-devices, programmable core types), while CreateKernel, L124 is the free function you call to attach a kernel to a program. The implementation behind it is where the years live: Device::initialize, L553 wires up the process-wide MetalContext, L150, the allocator, and the dispatch firmware.

One detail worth pausing on is what a “kernel” is here. Tensix cores contain several small RISC-V processors per tile, and tt-metal lets you program them individually. enum DataMovementProcessor, L23 names them: RISCV_0 is BRISC, RISCV_1 is NCRISC, and a compute kernel runs on the TRISC set. So one ttnn matmul typically becomes several cooperating binaries per core, talking through circular buffers. This is a very different mental model from one big CUDA kernel, and it explains why the repo carries its own kernel sources next to every C++ operation.

The ttnn/ tree mirrors the same split. Public headers like class Tensor, L30 define the value types, ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/ hosts hundreds of operations, and ttnn/ttnn/ is the Python package. The generic machinery in launch, L606 is the interesting part: every device operation funnels through one templated launch path that validates inputs, reuses cached programs, and eventually calls EnqueueMeshWorkload, L227 on the device’s mesh command queue. A single card is just a one-chip mesh, which is why mesh abstractions like class MeshDevice, L72 are not optional extras; they are the normal case.

The Python-to-C++ Seam

The binding layer uses nanobind rather than pybind11, and it is disciplined about ordering. NB_MODULE(_ttnn, mod), L233 comments explain why: every class and enum must be bound before any function that uses them as arguments. That is why the module first registers types such as the BufferType enum, L79 (DRAM, L1, L1_SMALL, TRACE), then binds operation functions.

Operations take one of two routes into Python. Newer, “C++-first” ops like matmul are bound wholesale on the C++ side, as in bind_function “matmul”, L693, docstrings and program-config types included. The Python layer then does almost nothing except re-export and attach a golden function: a pure-torch implementation used for correctness comparisons, registered through REGISTERED_OPERATIONS, L1751. That registry also powers ttnn.query_registered_operations(), a neat introspection surface few frameworks offer.

Device management crosses the same seam. open_device, L44 in Python is literally an alias for the bound ttnn._ttnn.device.open_device, documented in the device bindings, L73. And when you convert data with ttnn.from_torch(..., device=device), the wrapper at def from_torch, L282 creates the tensor, applies layout and dtype, and may immediately upload it through a command queue. Compared with the hand-written binding files we saw in MLX, this is a much more industrial setup: the seam is wide, typed, and mostly machine-repetition rather than glue hacks.

How an Op Becomes Silicon Work

Follow matmul deeper and the layered discipline pays off. The C++ wrapper at matmul.cpp forwards to a primitive; the primitive is a generic DeviceOperation; the operation picks a factory; and the factory does the real work of hardware mapping. The mcast-1D factory, for example, decides which cores multicast A’s tiles, which cores hold B’s shards, and which compute kernels consume both, calling tt_metal::CreateKernel, L634 once per kernel role. Each of those corresponds to an actual .cpp kernel source under device/kernels/, like the compute kernel at kernel_main, L20 and its data-movement counterpart at kernel_main, L14.

Once the program exists, dispatch takes over. FDMeshCommandQueue::enqueue_mesh_workload, L407 is the fast-dispatch front door, and assemble_device_commands, L2417 turns the program into a compact command sequence: launch messages, runtime-argument writes, semaphore updates. Those commands go into a host-side ring buffer managed by SystemMemoryManager, L123, which the card reads over PCIe. Two firmware kernels on reserved cores do the rest: a prefetcher at kernel_main, L3284 streams command pages downstream, and the dispatcher at kernel_main, L1589 executes them, writing kernel binaries and arguments to worker cores over the NOC. Even addresses come from a hardware abstraction: class Hal, L391 is populated per architecture by files like Hal::initialize_wh, L243 for Wormhole.

The elegance is that dispatch is itself a program on the same chip. There is no privileged host daemon copying work into a magic doorbell; the “driver” is firmware you can read, in this same repository.

Memory: Banks, Buffers, and Tiles

Memory is where tt-metal’s opinions get sharp. Every allocation is a class Buffer, L154, created through BufferImpl::create, L542, which asks the allocator for addresses. The allocator splits DRAM and L1 into banks managed by BankManager, L74, so an interleaved tensor is really a round-robin of pages across banks to spread bandwidth. Sharded layouts skip the round-robin and pin each core’s data to its own L1 region, which is what makes big matmuls and attention fast here.

The other half of the story is tilization. The matrix engine does not consume rows and columns; it consumes 32x32 tiles. That means every tensor has a logical shape and a padded physical shape, and layout conversion is a first-class operation. On the host, to_tile_major_layout, L206 does the conversion for CPU-resident data. On the device, a dedicated kernel at kernel_main, L26 performs the same trick as part of an op graph. Kernels exchange these tiles through circular buffers, tt-metal’s producer-consumer primitive, which is why program factories spend so much code choosing circular-buffer sizes. If you have read about warp-level tiling in CUTLASS, this is the same idea with different vocabulary, except here the tile size is fixed by the hardware and the compiler never hides it from you.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickest path is a wheel: the ttnn README documents pip install ttnn for machines with Tenstorrent hardware and drivers already set up. Building from source is the honest path for reading along: clone the repository, run ./build_metal.sh (the root CMake build), and the Python extension is produced from the same tree you just read. There is also a dockerfile directory if you want a hermetic environment.

The APIs used below are all taken from the repo’s own tutorial script, so this snippet is exactly what the library expects to work:

import torch
import ttnn

device = ttnn.open_device(device_id=0)

a = ttnn.from_torch(
    torch.rand(32, 32), dtype=ttnn.bfloat16,
    layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device,
)
b = ttnn.from_torch(
    torch.rand(32, 32), dtype=ttnn.bfloat16,
    layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device,
)

out = ttnn.matmul(a, b, memory_config=ttnn.DRAM_MEMORY_CONFIG)
print(ttnn.to_torch(out))

ttnn.close_device(device)

Three details connect back to the source tour. First, layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT is you opting into tilization at upload time, saving an on-device conversion. Second, memory_config=ttnn.DRAM_MEMORY_CONFIG is the interleaved layout managed by the BankManager allocator. Third, ttnn.matmul here runs the whole chain from the overview diagram: nanobind to C++ op to program factory to dispatch firmware. The same pattern scales up: the repo’s models/ tree contains ported networks, and if you want to see where such a runtime sits in a bigger system, our tours of MLC-LLM and ONNX Runtime cover the layers above.

Honest Limits

No hardware, no execution. Everything dispatch-related in this post was read, not run: tt-metal targets Tenstorrent cards (Wormhole, Blackhole, and newer), and the CI constantly exercises real silicon. Without a card you can still build and inspect, but the first open_device will not get far. That is inherent to the project, not a flaw, but it makes the curve steeper than for stacks where rented GPUs are everywhere.

The tree moves fast enough that line numbers are a perishable commodity. The dispatch internals have clearly been refactored recently; command-queue code now lives under several directories, and the Metal 2 host-API work is reshaping program construction. Any anchor cited here reflects the main branch at the time of writing and will drift.

Kernel coverage in ttnn is broad but uneven. Many ops accept program configs that dramatically change which factory runs, and the fallback-to-torch golden path exists precisely because some composite behavior is easier to verify than to reimplement. Reading ttnn.matmul alone involves thousands of lines across six factories; this tour follows one representative path rather than all of them.

Finally, the firmware kernels are long, dense C++ with compile-time constants from the HAL, and the prefetcher file alone runs past three thousand lines. The abstractions are honest, but the bottom of the stack is still the bottom: sometimes you read constexpr address arithmetic written for a chip, not for a reader. That is the price of a driver and a tensor library sharing one repository, and it is what makes tt-metal one of the few places where you can see the whole road from import ttnn to a RISC-V core doing arithmetic.
entry.summary: How ttnn's Python tensor ops cross nanobind into C++, become tt-metalium Programs, and land on Tensix RISC-V cores through Tenstorrent's fast-dispatch firmware.

entry.title: Inside Microsoft’s BitNet: Ternary Lookup-Table Kernels on CPU and CUDA

link.title: Inside Microsoft’s BitNet: Ternary Lookup-Table Kernels on CPU and CUDA

entry.content:
Two years of quantization work have convinced most teams that 4-bit is the practical floor for running large language models on everyday hardware. Microsoft’s BitNet refuses that floor entirely. Its weights live in {-1, 0, +1}, roughly 1.58 bits each, and the repository we are touring today is the official runtime for them. We looked at what BitNet is back in April in the conceptual overview; this time we walk the source itself, from a HuggingFace checkpoint all the way to lookup-table matrix multiplications executing inside a patched llama.cpp.

The interesting part of this codebase is not the transformers — those are ordinary — but the machinery around them. A build-time code generator emits AVX2 GEMM kernels as C++ text, a conversion tool reorders ternary weights into exactly the layout those kernels want, and a thin C++ shim overrides ggml’s mul_mat so llama.cpp runs BitNet kernels without knowing it. There is also a parallel GPU path where a pure PyTorch model calls hand-written CUDA kernels through ctypes. If you have read our tours of DeepSpeed’s ragged inference engine, TVM’s Relax VM, or Triton, this sits at a very different point on the same spectrum: almost no abstraction, maximal specialization per model shape.

Everything below links to real files on main. Diagrams first, then sections.

The BitNet ternary stack: setup and entry scripts at the left, checkpoint conversion and kernel codegen in the middle, generated AVX2/NEON kernels feeding a patched llama.cpp, with a pure-PyTorch CUDA detour below.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • setup_env.py orchestrates everything once: it quantizes the checkpoint, invokes codegen, and compiles a patched llama.cpp (compile).
  • run_inference.py and run_inference_server.py are thin wrappers that drive the resulting llama-cli and llama-server binaries.
  • convert-hf-to-gguf-bitnet.py packs ternary weights into three on-disk layouts: I2_S, TL1 and TL2.
  • codegen_tl2.py and codegen_tl1.py emit AVX2 and NEON lookup-table kernels; gemm-config.h holds the tiling knobs.
  • The generated headers live in preset_kernels and are included by ggml-bitnet-lut.cpp, the mul_mat override.
  • On GPU, gpu/model.py implements the transformer in PyTorch and calls bitnet_kernels.cu through ctypes.
  • e2e_benchmark.py times the whole thing end to end.

One Checkpoint, Three Layouts

The conversion tool, convert-hf-to-gguf-bitnet.py, is the quiet hero of this repository. It subclasses the llama.cpp GGUF exporter — see the Model base class at line 48 — but its BitnetModel subclass at line 1031 carries a scale_map (line 1077) that matches each linear layer to its precomputed activation scale. Ternary models throw away weight magnitudes, so the activation scales become the only thing keeping the forward pass calibrated; losing one layer’s scale is a silent quality disaster, and the map is how the tool avoids it.

Three output layouts fall out of one pass. The first is I2_S: quantize_to_i2_s maps {-1, 0, 1} to {0, 1, 2} (line 700), packs four ternary values into every byte (lines 705-725), and appends a 32-byte float32 scale tail per superblock. That is the format llama-quantize understands, which is why prepare_model in setup_env.py can finish the job by invoking the stock quantizer with the I2_S ftype (lines 145-152). Clever reuse: BitNet gets a standard GGUF file instead of inventing a container format.

The other two layouts, TL1 and TL2, are not about compression at all — they are about access order. transform_to_tl1 and transform_to_tl2 reorder and re-encode weights so that the lookup-table kernels of the next section can stream them sequentially. The preprocessing helpers (TL1 at line 483, TL2 at line 601) split each weight matrix into the block shapes the generated code will iterate over. If you have ever wondered why you cannot just run the stock gguf through the LUT path, this is why: the weights on disk are pre-shuffled for a specific kernel.

Codegen: Writing AVX2 Kernels at Build Time

Instead of hand-writing SIMD kernels for every supported model, BitNet writes Python that writes C++. codegen_tl2.py is the x86 half. Its gen_tbl_impl emits functions like three_tbl_impl_0 (line 287) — precomputed 256-entry lookup tables where each entry is the dot product of one 8-bit activation chunk with all possible ternary weight patterns. Since a ternary byte only takes 3^9-ish meaningful patterns, a multiply-accumulate chain collapses into table lookups plus integer adds.

The GEMM emitters, three_qgemm_lut and two_qgemm_lut, bake the model’s exact block sizes into the emitted loops, and gen_top_api wraps it all with the ggml_preprocessor glue (line 534) that ggml will call. The per-layer constructors from gen_ctor_code wire kernel selection to layer dimensions. docs/codegen.md shows the knobs: --BM, --BK, --bm control the tiling that gets hard-coded into the emitted loops.

How specific is the output? Compare the checked-in preset TL2 header for the 3B model: it guards itself with GGML_BITNET_X86_TL2, defines BK2 32 (line 24), and opens with hand-managed aligned allocators and _mm256 merge helpers (line 26). Every preset directory in preset_kernels/ is a frozen codegen output for one released model. Meanwhile gemm-config.h supplies compile-time tile constants per ISA — AVX2 gets row block 4, column block 128, parallel 4 (lines 3-10) — with NEON-DOTPROD and portable fallbacks below.

This is the same trade TVM made in our Relax VM tour, just at zero abstraction cost: TVM compiles arbitrary schedules through a compiler stack; BitNet stamps out one template with tuned constants. Less general, dramatically simpler, and for a fixed family of ternary transformer shapes, that simplicity wins.

The ggml mul_mat Override

The generated kernels need a host, and the host is ggml-bitnet-lut.cpp — about two hundred lines of glue that hooks into llama.cpp’s compute graph. Initialization (ggml_bitnet_init) allocates per-tensor extra state, and do_permutate applies a runtime row permutation to the in-memory weights, aligning them with the access pattern the generated loops assume.

Dispatch is guarded twice before any kernel runs. can_mul_mat checks the tensor type and device, and mul_mat_get_wsize computes the exact scratch size the qgemm needs — llama.cpp allocates work buffers once per graph, so this sizing function is what lets the LUT path request a different workspace than the stock matmul would. Only then does mul_mat run: it pulls the packed qlut data (line 107), the lut_scales and lut_biases (lines 108-109) that were stashed during init, and hands everything to the shape-matched generated function. Scales and biases ride along because the lookup tables hold raw integer accumulations; dequantization happens after the adds, in float.

Note what is absent: no dispatcher framework, no backend registry, no plugin API. When we toured ONNX Runtime we counted the layers of indirection between a node and its kernel; here it is one function with an if-chain. The cost is equally clear — the file knows llama.cpp internals intimately, so upstream ggml changes can break it, which is exactly why the repo pins its 3rdparty llama.cpp checkout.

The GPU Detour: Pure PyTorch Plus ctypes

The gpu/ directory is a second, independent implementation. Here the transformer is plain PyTorch — Attention, FeedForward, TransformerBlock built on xformers kernels — except every linear is a BitLinearKernel. Its forward quantizes activations to int8 per token (lines 68-71), then calls bitnet_int8xint2_linear, which loads libbitnet.so via ctypes (line 19) and passes raw data_ptr()s plus the current CUDA stream. No torch extension bindings, no autograd bookkeeping — inference only, and it shows.

The CUDA side mirrors the CPU story at smaller scale. bitnet_kernels.cu exports one C symbol, bitlinear_int8xint2, whose body is a chain of shape checks: each known (M, N, K) launches ladder_int8xint2_kernel with tile parameters chosen offline for that layer’s dimensions (lines 4-33). Weights arrive pre-packed as int8 (four ternary values per byte), so the kernel does its own unpack and int8-times-int2 accumulation, writing bf16 output. setup.py builds it as a bare CUDAExtension.

Around it, FastGen does what torch.compile was built for in our Executorch tour: compile_prefill and compile_generate trace the model into CUDA graphs, then generate_all replays them token by token with a KV cache managed by make_cache. The honest caveat: this path only supports the exact layer shapes hard-coded in the kernel dispatch — feed it an unknown width and the kernel prints a warning and skips the GEMM.

From Install to Your First Model

The intended flow is one command: setup_env.py detects your platform (system_info at line 90), pulls the model (get_model_name at line 93), quantizes it, runs codegen via gen_code, and invokes cmake with your chosen compiler (lines 220-222). After that, run_inference.py defaults to the bundled bitnet_b1_58-3B I2_S gguf with a 2048-token context and temperature 0.8, or you can serve it through run_inference_server.py on localhost:8080. Quality checking is built in too — PerplexityTester scores checkpoints against wikitext, and e2e_benchmark.py wraps timed CLI runs.

Being straight about the limits, because the source is: the generated and preset kernels are shape-pinned, so new model widths require a codegen run (docs/codegen.md shows the TL1 and TL2 invocations) and ideally a tuning sweep with GemmTuner, which searches configurations into kernel_config.ini (generate_configurations at line 262). Batch size 1 is the design point; the CUDA kernels literally check M == 1. And the patched llama.cpp is pinned, not merged — you are building a fork by design.

That trade is the whole point. BitNet buys CPU-side 3B-model inference at interactive speeds by refusing generality everywhere else: weights pre-shuffled on disk, kernels stamped out per model, one entry point that does everything. Compare it with the serving-grade generality of vLLM, the embedding focus of Text Embeddings Inference, the int8 CPU story of faster-whisper, or the self-hosted API surface of LocalAI — BitNet is the narrowest of the family and the only one betting the model format itself on ternary weights. For the conceptual background, start with our first BitNet post; for the other end of the efficiency spectrum, see our inference index.
entry.summary: A source tour of Microsoft's BitNet inference framework: how convert-hf-to-gguf-bitnet packs ternary weights, how codegen_tl2 emits AVX2 lookup-table GEMM kernels, and how a patched llama.cpp executes them on CPU and GPU.
